# Backlog

One task equals one commit equals one change that leaves the tree green. If a
task cannot be finished in one green commit, split it before writing code.

Task IDs are stable. Completed tasks stay here with their commit reference so
the history of why something was done survives.

**The current milestone's section is first; finished milestones follow it, most
recent first.** ⚠️ Written down rather than left to convention, because
`scripts/lib.sh` deliberately does *not* derive the current milestone from this
file's headings — it derives it from the commits, and its own comment says
reading the last heading instead "would only trade that for a dependency on an
unwritten ordering convention". Nothing reads the order; `next-task` reads "the
top unblocked task" and a human reads the top of the file, and both want the
milestone actually being built.

Decomposition rule: only the current milestone is decomposed in detail. Future
milestones stay as [roadmap](roadmap.md) entries with a
[plan](milestones/README.md) until their turn. ⚠️ **A plan is not a
decomposition** — it is a hypothesis, it carries no task IDs, and its items are
re-derived rather than copied when a milestone opens. Read the plan's
"Decisions required first" before writing any of that milestone's code; see
[`sdd.md`](../standards/sdd.md) §Decomposition.

## M12: Admin API and operability

19 rows against a plan of 19. ADR-0058 resolves the opening decisions: topic
listing remains principal-scoped, admin and group operations deny by default,
deletion is a durable non-reusable tombstone, unsupported configuration is
refused, routine telemetry is bounded, and role selection changes real
responsibilities. A finding filed while M12 runs is dispositioned when filed
(`milestone/SKILL.md`).

## M8: Encryption, BYOK, and the key seam

⚠️ **17 rows against a plan of 18** (`M8.10`-`M8.12` opened by `M8.1`-`M8.3`'s reviews, `M8.13`-`M8.14` by `M8.4`'s, `M8.15` by the development-loop review, and `M8.16` by the checkpoint review): `ADR-0050` defers FR-41's real-cloud round trip to M15 and FR-43 (the FIPS build) to M13, whose task 5 already owns that build job, and this section builds what remains — the envelope, the nonce type, the DEK cache, key-domain segregation and both providers against simulations. A finding filed while M8 runs is dispositioned when filed (`milestone/SKILL.md`).

| ID | Task | Acceptance | State |
|---|---|---|---|
| M8.0 | M8's opening: the decisions, the decomposition, and the red completion gate | Serves no FR/NFR. Records `ADR-0050` (the envelope scheme, the nonce type, DEK rotation at 64 GiB or 7 days, lazy re-wrap, defined revocation, and what M8 verifies versus defers — ⚠️ taken without the user's answer, overridable); writes `scripts/gates/m8-complete.sh` red, one leg per clause it can assert plus the nonce leg; flips M7 `complete` and M8 `in progress`; hands FR-41's vendor round trip to M15 and FR-43 to M13 in `roadmap.md`'s deferral table and each receiving plan. Acceptance: `check-milestone-exit.sh` and `check-milestone-handoff.sh` green, and the gate runs red. | done |
| M8.1 | Key material that cannot leak or linger | Serves FR-44, NFR-33 — `M8.md` tasks 1, 6. A `Dek` newtype in `oqueue-core` beside `WrappedKey`, zeroized on drop, with `Redacted`'s equality made constant-time. Acceptance: a `Dek` dropped leaves no copy of its bytes in the buffer it owned; `Debug` on `Dek`, `WrappedKey` and any error carrying them prints no key material; `check-secrets.sh` covers the new fields. ⚠️ **Done**: `Dek` is a 32-byte newtype in `oqueue-core` with no `Clone` and no `PartialEq`, a fixed-string `Debug`, constant-time `ct_eq` via `subtle`, and `Drop`/`ZeroizeOnDrop` via `zeroize`; `Redacted`'s derived `PartialEq`/`Eq` are replaced by a constant-time impl bounded on `T: AsRef<[u8]>`, and it gained `Zeroize` but still does **not** zeroize on drop (conditional `Drop` needs specialization, and a `Drop` impl would forbid `expose_into`) — documented on the type. ⚠️ The zeroize test calls `zeroize()`, the same function `Drop` calls, and asserts all 32 bytes are zero: it proves the wipe reaches every byte and (by a compile-time `ZeroizeOnDrop` bound) that the type promises it on drop; it does **not** observe memory after the drop, which is unreachable without `unsafe`. `check-secrets.sh` gained a `dek` root and a `key_material` substring, and accepts `Dek`/`WrappedKey` beside `Redacted` as safe carriers. | done |
| M8.2 | A nonce no call sequence can repeat | Serves FR-42 — `ADR-0050` point 2, `M8.md` task 5. Writer epoch ‖ object sequence ‖ region index as a type with no byte-wise constructor. Acceptance: `no_call_sequence_repeats_a_nonce` is a property test over any sequence of nonce-producing calls; two regions of one object, two objects of one writer and two writers all differ. ⚠️ **Done**: `nonce.rs` makes every level linear — `NonceMinter` (one per writer epoch) owns the only object-sequence counter and `NonceSource::new` is private, so no caller can name an object sequence; `NonceSource` hands out regions from a counter that only advances, so a second ask is `NonceRegionOutOfOrder` rather than a repeat; neither type is `Clone`. Sealing takes a minted `Nonce`, opening takes a decoded `ParsedNonce`, and there is no path between them. Bit layout, big-endian 12 bytes: writer epoch (40 bits, bytes 0-4) ‖ object sequence (40 bits, bytes 5-9) ‖ region index (16 bits, bytes 10-11); every out-of-range input is refused, never truncated, so the map is injective. The one obligation left to a caller is a writer epoch distinct across restarts — `M8.10`. ⚠️ **And the nonce value itself is linear** (second review round): `Nonce` is neither `Clone` nor `Copy`, so a flush whose upload failed cannot silently re-seal different bytes under the nonce still in scope — a seal consumes it. | done |
| M8.3 | Seal and open one region, with the algorithm read from the header | Serves FR-43's agnostic half, NFR-14 — `M8.md` tasks 4, 7. AES-256-GCM in `oqueue-crypto` (no I/O, `forbid(unsafe_code)`), selected at open time from `RegionAlg`, never assumed. Acceptance: a sealed region opens to its plaintext; a tampered ciphertext, tag, nonce or `alg` is refused rather than misread; an unknown `alg` is an error, not a default. ⚠️ **Done**: `oqueue-crypto::region` seals and opens one region with AES-256-GCM (RustCrypto `aes-gcm` 0.11, `default-features = false`, no `getrandom` — pure Rust, no build script in any of the twelve crates it adds or the eighteen `Cargo.toml` audits), dispatching on the `RegionAlg` read from the header; `RegionAlg::Aes256Gcm = 1` joins `None = 0`, `from_code` still refuses anything else, and a region that is not sealed still writes 0. The AAD binds the region's identity — a domain prefix, the length-prefixed topic name, the partition, the region index, the record count and the algorithm code — and deliberately not the object key, byte range or wrapped DEK, so a region stays movable between objects of the same identity until `M8.4` brings the footer under the tag. Overhead is exactly `TAG_BYTES = 16`, GCM's untruncated tag, appended after the ciphertext. | done |
| M8.4 | The envelope in the footer | Serves FR-41, FR-42 — `M8.md` task 7. A sealed region's footer carries `{key_id, wrapped_dek, nonce, alg}`; the unsealed shape is byte-identical to what M3 writes today. Acceptance: round trip through `parse_footer`; an object with no sealed region has the same bytes as before this row; the footer fuzz target covers the new shape.  ⚠️ **Carries `M8.12`'s obligation**: bring the region header's own bytes under a tag as far as the format allows. ⚠️ **Done**. **The format decision: no version bump, and the `alg` byte is the discriminator.** A region with `alg = 0` encodes exactly the bytes it always did — pinned by `an_object_with_no_sealed_region_is_byte_identical_to_what_the_tree_wrote_before` against a 217-byte literal *derived from the documented shape*, not pasted from a run — and a region with `alg != 0` is followed by `u16 key_id_len ‖ key_id ‖ u32 wrapped_len ‖ wrapped ‖ 12-byte nonce`. `BUNDLE_FORMAT_VERSION` stays `1` because this format has **no** forward compatibility: `parse_footer` refuses any version it does not know, so a bump is a hard cut that would have made every *unsealed* object unreadable to today's readers to describe a change none of them carry. ⚠️ **What an older reader does with a sealed footer is stated rather than guaranteed** (`bundle/encode.rs`'s header): it reads the envelope as the next region's fields and fails in almost every case, and the honest guarantee is instead that **no object with `alg = 1` exists** until `M8.6` writes one. ⚠️ **Under the tag**: topic, partition, region index, algorithm code and record count (all `M8.3`/`M8.13`) **plus the key id** — so a footer relabelled to another tenant's KEK or a forged count does not open. The **nonce** is bound by AES-GCM itself rather than by the AAD, which is why it is not duplicated there. ⚠️ **Outside the tag, and it is the wrapped DEK's bytes alone**: `ADR-0050` point 4's lazy re-wrap changes them for an unchanged key, so binding them would make every re-wrap a decrypt-and-reseal — the argument was re-examined, not inherited, and what it concedes is bounded (substituting them gives an unwrap failure or a different DEK, and a different DEK fails the tag: a denial of service on one region, never a region opening as something it is not). The **byte range** stays outside because compaction changes it without changing the records. ⚠️ **`alg = 1 → 0` is still `M8.12`'s**: the parser refuses that edit only because the envelope's bytes then misparse, which is a consequence of the layout rather than a guarantee about the byte. Bounds: a `u16` key id and a wrapped DEK bounded by `MAX_WRAPPED_DEK_LEN` (8 KiB), both checked **before** anything is copied, on the write path and against a *claimed* length on the read path. Two fuzz seeds added (`one-sealed-region`, `sealed-and-unsealed`). ⚠️ Also: a composite manifest has no envelope field, so both its writer and its parser now **refuse** a sealed region rather than dropping the envelope silently. | done |
| M8.5 | One DEK per topic, rotated on bytes or time, cached both ways | Serves NFR-33 — `M8.md` tasks 8, 9. A write-side cache rotating at whichever of 64 GiB or 7 days comes first, and a read-side cache of unwrapped DEKs keyed by the wrapped blob with a TTL. Acceptance: `kms_calls_follow_rotation_not_produce_volume` holds KMS calls flat as produce volume grows tenfold and shows one wrap per rotation; a read of many objects under one DEK unwraps once. ⚠️ **Done** (`M8.5`): `DEK_MAX_SEALED_BYTES` = 64 GiB and `DEK_MAX_AGE_MS` = 7 days on the write side, `UNWRAPPED_DEK_TTL_MS` = 5 minutes and `UNWRAPPED_DEK_CACHE_ENTRIES` = 1024 on the read side, all four pinned in `check-drift.sh`'s `RUST_BOUNDS` with *raising* named as the weakening direction. ⚠️ The capacity is not a tuning knob: expiry is noticed by a lookup and eviction only by an insert, so without it an entry nobody reads again keeps a plaintext DEK resident for the life of the process — the read that found that is in this row's review. Fresh key material comes from a new seam, `oqueue_crypto::Entropy` — `OsEntropy` over `getrandom` (a new direct dependency, no build script, no host tool, argued in the workspace root) for production, `FakeEntropy` (a counter, and loudly not entropy) for tests, so no library code calls the OS RNG and no DEK is derived from a counter in production. The read cache is keyed by `(key id, wrapped blob)`, never by topic. | done |
| M8.6 | A topic's key domain, and a flush that never spans two | Serves FR-42, NFR-14 — `M8.md` tasks 12, 13, 14. A per-topic KEK reference in the catalog entry, and a flush planner routing each topic's regions to its key domain's object. Acceptance: `no_object_mixes_key_domains` over a mixed workload; `byok_topics_leave_the_default_path_untouched` asserts a default topic's object bytes and store operations are what they were with no BYOK topic present.  ⚠️ **`M8.12` must land with or before this row**: writing `alg=1` is what makes the downgrade reachable. | done |
| M8.7 | Both providers, one seam | Serves FR-41 — `M8.md` tasks 10, 11, `ADR-0050` point 6. AWS KMS `Encrypt`/`Decrypt` and GCP Cloud KMS `encrypt`/`decrypt`, never `GenerateDataKey`, each against an in-process simulation of its API. Acceptance: `both_kms_providers_round_trip_through_one_seam` wraps with one and unwraps with the same, through `dyn KeyProvider`, with the same test body for both. ⚠️ **Done** (`M8.7`): `AwsKmsProvider` and `GcpKmsProvider` map separate encrypt/decrypt API traits into the same `KeyProvider` contract; one `assert_round_trip` body runs against both simulations and refuses a wrapped DEK under another key id. Neither adapter has a `generate_data_key` path, and real vendor round trips remain M15's. | done |
| M8.8 | Revocation and re-seal, never a stuck queue | Serves FR-41, FR-42 — `ADR-0050` points 4, 5, `M8.md` task 15. Compaction re-seals within a key domain and preserves the topic→key association; a revoked KEK makes reads fail with a specific error, makes compaction skip that domain recording why, and refuses produce rather than writing plaintext. Acceptance: a test per behaviour, and one asserting a revoked domain does not stall compaction of any other. ⚠️ **Done** (`ADR-0057`): `oqueue-compact` accepts a domain/re-sealer policy, validates the domain before copying, re-seals customer regions with output-position context, and emits the returned sealed bytes through `BundleStream::push_sealed`; `Error::KeyRevoked` is non-retryable and is propagated unchanged, so a caller can record the reason and continue another domain. Tests prove the returned ciphertext and wrapped envelope are used, reads surface revocation, and a revoked domain is followed by a successful default-domain merge. | done |
| M8.10 | A writer epoch that cannot repeat across a restart | Serves FR-42 — opened by `M8.2`, which found the gap and documented it rather than hiding it. `Nonce`'s uniqueness rests on three conditions and the type can enforce only one; the other two are the composer's. `WriterId::mint` remains a string for object naming, while `WriterEpoch` now accepts only a durable allocator result, so a node cannot feed a pid, wall-clock stamp, or shared coordinator fence into nonce construction. Acceptance: the epoch a `NonceSource` is opened with cannot repeat for a given key domain across restarts (derived from the coordinator's fenced term, the lease, or a durable counter — whichever the composer can guarantee), with a test that a restarted node seals under a different epoch, and `ADR-0050` records the derivation. ⚠️ **Done** (`M8.10`, superseded by `M8.16`): `NonceMinter` first required a typed coordinator epoch and proved the restart shape; the follow-up replaces that insufficient shared source with `DurableWriterEpochAllocator`, and `a_restarted_writer_uses_a_new_durable_epoch` keeps the core refusal boundary. ⚠️ **Blocks sealing in production**: no topic may be sealed until this holds. | done |
| M8.11 | SASL password comparison is constant time | Serves FR-40, FR-44 — carried from `M9` (`sasl_authenticate.rs`'s own module header names M8 as the owner) and found again by `M8.1`. The PLAIN path compares with `==` on the exposed string, so it leaks the length of the matching prefix by timing; `Redacted`'s equality became constant-time in `M8.1` and this path bypasses it. Acceptance: the comparison goes through the constant-time path, with a test that a wrong password of the right length and a wrong password of the wrong length take the same code path, and the module header's claim is removed rather than left standing. ⚠️ **Done**: the PLAIN verifier uses `Redacted::ct_eq_bytes`, with equal- and different-length wrong-password refusal tests covering the path. | done |
| M8.12 | A region's sealed-ness is not a byte an attacker can clear | Serves FR-42, FR-43 — `M8.3`'s review, major in substance, minor in reach today. The algorithm lives in the region header, and the header is outside the tag: editing `alg` from `1` to `0` never reaches `open` at all — `parse_footer` accepts it, the reader sees `RegionAlg::None` and serves ciphertext to a consumer as record batches, with no tag checked. ⚠️ **`from_code` accepting `1` has already removed the fail-closed refusal**, a commit before any reader honours it: `oqueue-broker/src/region.rs` and `oqueue-compact/src/merge.rs` used to reject `alg=1` as unknown and now pass those bytes through as batches. Unreachable while nothing writes `1`, and reachable the moment `M8.6` does. Acceptance: a reader derives whether a region must be sealed from its topic's key domain rather than from the header byte, and refuses a region whose header says `none` in a domain that requires sealing; a test edits the byte and asserts the refusal; `M8.4`'s footer brings the header's own bytes under a tag where it can. ⚠️ **Done**: `KeyDomain::validate_region` is the fail-closed boundary used by broker slicing and compaction; default-domain readers accept only unsealed regions, customer-key readers require a sealed region and matching key id, and mismatches are non-retryable. | done |
| M8.13 | The region's record count belongs in the associated data | Serves FR-42 — `M8.4`'s review. `M8.4` excluded the record count from the AAD "for the same reason the byte range is not", and that reason is true only of the byte range: compaction relocates sealed bytes without decrypting, so a region's **record count is invariant across every rewrite the design permits**, and binding it is free. Today an edited footer `record_count` still opens, so the reader assigns offsets from a count the ciphertext does not match. Acceptance: the record count is in `RegionAad::encode`, the pinned vectors are regenerated, and a test edits the count and asserts the refusal. ⚠️ **Done**: `record_count` is encoded between `region_index` and `alg`, both pinned vectors carry the new bytes, and editing the count fails authentication before offsets can be assigned. | done |
| M8.14 | A parsed `KeyId` is not a log-injection payload | Serves FR-42, NFR-51 — `M8.4`'s review. `KeyId::new` accepts any non-empty UTF-8, and `region_envelope.rs` lets a footer carry up to `MAX_KEY_ID_LEN` (65535) bytes of it, while `key.rs` documents a key id as ⚠️ *safe to log, and the thing to log instead of anything that is not*. A forged id containing newlines is therefore a log-injection payload at the first site that logs one, which `M8.5` onward is. Acceptance: `KeyId` validates its character set and length on construction from parsed bytes, a test asserts a newline-bearing id is refused, and the "safe to log" claim is either true or removed. ⚠️ **Done**: `KeyId` now accepts only non-empty printable ASCII identifiers no longer than the footer's `u16` length, so parsed footer values are safe to log and bounded before allocation; newline and oversize tests assert refusal without echoing the payload. | done |
| M8.15 | A milestone cannot grow past the reviewer's task budget | Serves no FR/NFR — ADR-0052. The 20-task limit in `sdd.md` is enforced for the active milestone rather than left as advice. Acceptance: `check-milestone-exit.sh` fails an in-progress milestone with 21 backlog rows and names handoff to the next milestone; the negative suite observes that failure; exactly 20 rows still passes. | done |
| M8.16 | Writers do not share a nonce epoch | Serves FR-42 — the M8 checkpoint review found that a coordinator fence is shared by multiple writer processes, so `WriterEpoch` derived from it alone lets each process restart object sequence zero under the same DEK. Acceptance: a durable object-store epoch allocator uses conditional create-only terms so two writers sharing one coordinator fence receive distinct epochs and a restarted allocator receives a later epoch; `NonceMinter` accepts only those durable epochs; a concurrent-allocation test proves no duplicate epoch. ⚠️ **Done** (`M8.16`): `DurableWriterEpochAllocator` stores immutable `writer-epoch/{term}` objects with `IfAbsent`, retries lost races, rejects malformed metadata and values beyond the 40-bit nonce field, and the latency-injected concurrent test proves two writers and a restart receive distinct terms. `WriterEpoch` no longer accepts a coordinator epoch; ADR-0055 supersedes ADR-0054. | done |
| M8.9 | M8's closing round | Serves no FR/NFR. A milestone review by an agent that did not drive M8; every finding dispositioned. Acceptance: `m8-complete.sh` exits 0. ⚠️ **Done**: Carver's whole-milestone review was recorded; its major spec finding is argued in `baselines/review.txt`, and its minor documentation contradiction is corrected in the M8.9 closure commit. | done |

⚠️ **14 rows against a plan of 17** (`M7.3a` split from `M7.3`; `M7.12` opened by the closing review): `ADR-0049` builds the part of `M7.md` its completion condition measures — a catalog the node looks up rather than holds, one shard behind a lookup, and the scale evidence — and hands the rest to M15 in `roadmap.md`'s deferral table. Three rows are received from M6 (`M7.8`-`M7.10`) because they are observable and sharding multiplies them; the other three M6 handed on go to M15 with the rest. | ID | Task | Acceptance | State |
|---|---|---|---|
| M7.0 | M7's opening: the decision, the decomposition, and the red completion gate | Serves no FR/NFR. Records `ADR-0049` (the catalog is looked up per shard, not held — ⚠️ taken without the user's answer, overridable); writes `scripts/gates/m7-complete.sh` red, one leg per clause of `M7.md`'s completion condition; flips M6 `complete` and M7 `in progress`; re-derives `M6.2`, `M6.16` and `M6.18` as `M7.8`-`M7.10` and marks them `dissolved`; hands `M6.9`, `M6.11`, `M6.12` and the rest of `M7.md`'s provisional list to M15. Acceptance: `check-milestone-exit.sh`, `check-milestone-handoff.sh` green and the gate runs red. | done |
| M7.1 | A topic's metadata shard is a lookup | Serves NFR-10 — `ADR-0049` point 1, `M7.md` task 1. `MetadataShardId` and a `ShardMap` answering topic → shard; every per-shard object prefix (`meta/`, `groups/`, `catalog/`) is derived from the id it returns rather than written as a literal. ## M5: Compaction and retention

⚠️ **65 rows against `sdd.md`'s 20-task cap, argued here because the standard
asks for the argument in this section's own notes.** The test the cap exists
for is whether these rows are one milestone, and the honest answer is that
**49 of them are M5's own work, 15 are debt this milestone received rather than
generated, and 1 is the opening bookkeeping**. ⚠️ **It was 38 when `M5.0`
wrote it and `M5.38`-`M5.64` are the rows that moved it.** ⚠️ **Each of those
says on its own row who opened it, and this paragraph deliberately does not
list them** — it did, three times, and went stale three times: `M5.43` items
(6) and (12) each corrected a count and a filer list here and each left the
next one wrong, which is the failure this paragraph exists to avoid reproduced
inside it. The rule that survives a row being added: **a row opened after the
decomposition names its own opener**, and there are three kinds — a per-commit
round's finding written as a row in the next commit — a minor under
`review.md` rule 15, or a defect the commit could not solve in its own scope
(`M5.44`) — this
milestone's own need for something the decomposition did not foresee

a whole rather than a delta (`M5.46`-`M5.50`), and the loop's own cost measured

is reviewed, so deferring them to a harness milestone would mean paying the cost
that opened them for the whole of `M5.7`-`M5.28`.

cap argument that accounts for only some of the rows is what `sdd.md` says the

  `M5.12`-`M5.15`), retention (`M5.16`-`M5.19`), deletion safety

  repacking is what stops one slow-expiring partition pinning the object, so
  compaction is what makes retention a *retention* requirement rather than an

| M5.1 | `read_amp(partition, range)` computed from the index | Serves FR-34. The trigger input, and the only one: objects touched by a fetch of `range` divided by the minimum that could serve it, read from the materialized index with no object-storage access. ⚠️ **Never triggered on object count** (`M5.md` task 1) — a partition whose many objects are never read together has no amplification to fix. Acceptance: a unit test where an index with one contiguous object over the range gives `read_amp == 1.0`, one where the same range is spread over 12 objects gives `12.0`, and — ⚠️ **amended by `M5.1` itself** — the no-store criterion held structurally rather than by a test: `read_amp` takes a `MaterializedIndex` and no store, so there is no store to hand it and no test can pass a panicking one. ⚠️ **The first version of this sentence also credited the dependency set and `check-sans-io.sh`, and both were false** — `M5.38`, filed by this task's own review, is where that is corrected and given a gate leg that actually holds it. What a test *can* constrain is the cost that criterion was reaching for, and one does: a counting index asserting the walk makes one query for a range one page covers. | done |
| M5.2 | Compaction planner: amplification threshold **and** an age guard | Serves FR-34. Selects `(partition, range)` where `read_amp` exceeds `COMPACTION_READ_AMP_THRESHOLD` (12, inside `M5.md`'s 8-16 starting band) **and** the range is older than the latency SLO, so tail data still served from cache is never rewritten. ⚠️ Both conditions, not either: the age guard is what makes `M5.md`'s "pure tail consumption" case cost nothing. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.2` itself: the guard is the tail/history tier boundary, not a wall clock, because this index holds no timestamp.** `IndexState`'s tail window is the hot tier by construction — byte ranges inline, one GET — so "in the tail" is the available spelling of "still served from cache", and an `ObjectRef` carrying a timestamp would cost 16 bytes against the ~40-byte budget doc 14 §3's arithmetic rests on. ⚠️ **The known gap, recorded rather than discovered later**: a partition that stops being written keeps its last `TAIL_WINDOW_ENTRIES` objects in the tail for ever, so an idle partition's tail is never compacted. `M5.16` is where the index gains `ts_min`/`ts_max` and the guard becomes time-based; its row carries the obligation to tighten this one. Acceptance: a table test over the four combinations of (over/under threshold) × (older/newer than the guard) asserting exactly one produces a plan; and a test that a partition whose data is already contiguous produces no plan at any age. | done |
| M5.3 | Per-plan cost estimate and budget gate | Serves FR-34. Every plan carries GET count, PUT count and records rewritten before it runs; a plan over `COMPACTION_PLAN_RECORDS_BUDGET` is refused or deferred rather than truncated, because a half-run merge is the one operation that can silently lose data. Acceptance: a test asserting a plan whose estimate exceeds the budget is not executed and is reported as deferred with its estimate, ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.3` itself**: the second criterion — the estimate equalling the executor's actual counts — cannot be met here, because the executor is `M5.4` and does not exist. `M5.4`'s row receives it. What this row proves instead is the arithmetic and the refusal: one GET per input, one PUT per output, records as the budgeted quantity, and an over-budget plan returned as `Deferred` carrying the estimate that refused it. ⚠️ **`puts` is one per output object, not one per multipart part** — `M5.6` sets the part size, so the number is a floor until then. ⚠️ **Bytes are struck, not merely renamed, and `M5.7` is the row that needed them** — its criterion asks that this estimate budget the egress a client-side copy pays, and egress is bytes. `M5.7`'s row now carries the consequence: whichever answer it takes must either bring a byte length with it or say in what unit it budgets. ⚠️ **Budgeted in records rather than bytes**, for the reason `COMPACTED_OBJECT_RECORDS` is: the history tier holds no byte range, so a byte budget would need a GET per candidate and the estimate would cost what it bounds. | done |

Exactly one additional GET per input regardless of its size, bounded memory, no random seeks. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.4` itself: bounded on the input side only.** The whole object is read once and the footer parsed out of the bytes already in hand — a separate tail read would double the request count on the one path whose cost model is request-bound — and reads are sequential, so one input's bytes are resident at a time. The *output* accumulated in a `BundleBuilder` and was PUT whole when this row landed, so peak memory was one input plus the whole output; ⚠️ **`M5.6` closed that and this sentence is past tense because of it** — `merge` opens a `BundleStream`, so peak memory is one input plus one part, and `M5.3`'s records budget bounds the work rather than the memory. `M5.6`'s row receives the obligation. ⚠️ **It also receives `M5.3`'s second criterion**, which that row could not meet for want of an executor: the estimate must equal the executor's actual counts. Acceptance: a test over inputs whose total size is 50x the configured memory bound asserting peak buffer occupancy stays under it; a test asserting GET count equals input count exactly — not input count plus a re-read; and a test asserting `CostEstimate::of` predicts the run's own GET and PUT counts for a plan that runs. ⚠️ **The 50x-memory-bound test is `M5.6`'s**, for the reason above: what this row can observe is one read in flight at a time and no read returning more than one input, and that is what its tests assert. ⚠️ **And the merge takes the plan, not a bare range** — an input straddling the plan's range is refused rather than copied whole, an object whose regions do not account for the record count the index recorded is refused, inputs are sorted by base offset here rather than trusted to arrive in order, and a unique output key per attempt is what keeps a retry off an object the index already names — ⚠️ **written `IfAbsent` when this row landed, and `M5.6` replaced that with the unique key** (`ADR-0037`), because the precondition caught a reused key instead of not reusing one. Every one of those is a way acknowledged records go missing with nothing failing (NFR-20), and each has a test that observes the refusal. ⚠️ **And the inputs must *tile* the plan's range** — sorting fixes their order and says nothing about coverage, so a list missing one object writes an output with those offsets absent and a list naming one twice writes them twice, both silent. The refs must start at the plan's start, end at its end, and each begin exactly where the last ended. ⚠️ **`COMPACTION_PLAN_RECORDS_BUDGET` drops from eight compacted objects to one in this commit**, because the merge writes one object and a larger budget let a plan be costed at two outputs and run as one — `M5.6`'s multipart writer is what earns the raise back. | done |

| M5.12 | Range-coverage check before every commit | Serves FR-34. Verify every input offset range is covered by the outputs before the swap. Cheap insurance on the one operation that can silently lose data. Acceptance: a test injecting an output set missing one offset range asserting the commit is refused and the inputs stay live — not a warning, a refusal. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.12` itself: the swap it guards is `M5.13`'s and does not exist yet**, so this ships `covers(retiring, installing)` — sans-I/O, a sort and a walk over two small reference lists — and the cases that pin it, rather than a check wired to nothing. ⚠️ **The rule is equality, not containment**: outputs covering *more* than the inputs are refused too, because those offsets are either records another reference still names — served twice once the swap lands — or records nothing else names, which compaction was not authorised to produce. ⚠️ **And retiring nothing is refused**, since installing without retiring is the write path adding records through the compaction seam, where none of the write path's checks are. ⚠️ **One contiguity rule, not two**: `merge`'s `tiling()` already checked the *input* side against the plan's range, and it now reads `contiguous_span` too — two notions of what a gap is, one per side, is the drift this check has to be free of. ⚠️ **And the first round found two holes the cases left open.** Missing a range at the *start* was unconstrained — weakening the rule to compare only the high offsets left every other case green, and `cargo-mutants` cannot reach it because its operators replace the whole comparison rather than one half. And an empty covering, every input filtered out as outside the plan's range, was admitted if the fallback fabricated the plan's own range: the merge then failed one step later on an unsealable empty bundle, so `expect_err` was satisfied by the defect. Both now have a case, and the second asserts *which* refusal rather than that one happened. ⚠️ **`covers` knows nothing about partitions and says so**: an `ObjectRef` carries no topic or partition, so a mixed set describes no range at all — the caller plans one partition at a time, which is where that obligation lives. | done |
| M5.13 | Atomic commit at the coordinator: one transaction swapping input refs for output refs | Serves FR-34, FR-11. ⚠️ Compaction must never affect correctness, only efficiency. ⚠️ **It receives `ADR-0037`'s unique-key obligation.** The streaming seal is unconditional, and what keeps a retry off an object an index entry already names is that no two attempts share a key — `merge` and `merge_round` take the key from their caller and nothing mints it today, so the guarantee is a convention until this row makes it a mechanism. ⚠️ **`M5.6` dropped an `IfAbsent` precondition to get here**, which was the weaker form of the same guarantee: it caught a reused key instead of not reusing one. Acceptance includes a test that two attempts at one plan write two keys and the index names exactly one. ⚠️ **It receives `M5.5`'s index-side criterion**: that a fetch over a compacted range resolves to exactly one `ObjectRef`, which only becomes true once the swap has happened. Acceptance: a test asserting a fetch over the compacted range resolves to one `ObjectRef` after the commit where it resolved to N before it; a test asserting a fetch concurrent with the swap returns the same records whichever side of it lands, and a test asserting a failure partway through the commit leaves the inputs live and the outputs orphaned rather than the reverse. ⚠️ **`ADR-0038` obligation 1 is an acceptance criterion here, not advice**: the swap is an **append** that leaves every original `BatchCommitted` event in the log, and rewrites or removes none of them. An idempotent producer's identity survives a compaction rewrite in the log and nowhere else — the footer carries none by design (`M11.5`) and a merged span holds records from several input spans with several identities — so a swap that rewrote those events would satisfy every other criterion on this row and every gate, and destroy the only thing `ADR-0038` rests on. It bites when `M6` builds the replay path `ReplayRequired` names. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.13` itself: this ships the record and the fold, not the key-minting mechanism.** `MetadataRecord::RangeCompacted { topic, partition, retiring, installing }` and `IndexState`'s refusal of it are the swap; the unique key `ADR-0037` obliges is `M5.75`'s, because `merge` takes its key from a caller that does not exist until the executor does. ⚠️ **The two-attempts acceptance is met by the fold rather than by the key**, which is the stronger half: a second attempt at one plan retires references the first already retired, so it is refused and its object is orphaned — the index names one whatever keys were used. ⚠️ **And `covers` moved to `oqueue-core`**: `M5.12` put it beside the merge that produces the outputs, and the *coordinator* is the caller, so it lives where the fold can read it and `oqueue-compact` re-exports nothing it did not already have. ⚠️ **Paging invariance is a property of this record too**, and it was not free: a swap retires *history* references while a commit appends to the *tail*, so a swap batched with the commits that demote its objects must see them — checked against the pre-batch index alone, the same log was refused in one page and accepted in several. ⚠️ **And the first round found three blocking defects with one root cause**: the check pass was a second description of the apply pass, and the two disagreed. Two swaps in one batch were both accepted (and refused one page at a time); a swap batched with a publication for the same partition left a manifest and a reference covering the same offsets; a chained pair was refused in one page and accepted in two. ⚠️ **So the fold no longer checks and then applies — it projects.** Each effect is applied, in log order, to a *clone* of the partition it touches, and the clone is installed only if every step succeeded: a check that is the fold cannot disagree with the fold. That removed `Publication`, `Swap`, `admissible`, `swappable`, `absorb_published`, `apply_swaps` and `boundary`'s staged parameter, along with the running `covered` value `M5.62`'s first round added — a decreasing publication is now refused because the projection has already absorbed the first. ⚠️ **Only partitions an effect touches are cloned**, which matters because a partition's history is thousands of references at doc 14 §3's working set (`ADR-0043`) and the commit path is the ack path: a produce batch carries no effects and clones nothing. ⚠️ **And the third round found a swap that spans exactly what it retires and still loses a record**: `installing` carrying a zero-record reference beside the real output. A reference covering no offsets is neither a gap nor an overlap, so the contiguity rule admitted it — and installed, it sorts into history *ahead of* the real object at the same base offset, where a fetch resuming there lands on the empty one, finds its end is not past the start, and resumes at the next object. Silent, and only from the offset a consumer actually resumes at. Found with a randomized differential harness over 1,199 seeds; `contiguous_span` refuses an empty reference now, on both sides. | done |

| M5.18 | Retention on idle partitions, on `ADR-0036`'s expiry heap | Serves FR-33 — the requirement's own acceptance criterion. A coordinator-side min-heap keyed `ts_min + retention`, popped by a retention round, rebuilt from the materialized index on start so it is derived state and never a second source of truth. Acceptance: a test that a partition receiving no write and no read for longer than its retention has its data deleted on schedule; a test asserting a round over 100k partitions with 3 expiring touches 3; and a test asserting a rebuilt heap produces the same deadlines as the one it replaced.  ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.18` itself: keyed on the newest commit, not the oldest, and it decides without acting.** The row keys the heap `ts_min + retention`, which is when a partition's oldest data could first expire. Keyed on `ts_min`, a busy partition's deadline fires every round and finds nothing it may trim; progressive trims of an active partition's oldest objects need per-object times, which is `M5.16`'s half. ⚠️ **A round returns `Trimmed` records; it does not journal them.** The coordinator journals only `BatchCommitted` today — nothing in production can append a trim, or compaction's `RangeCompacted` — so this row's first criterion, *data deleted on schedule*, is met at the index: the round trims on schedule, and deletion of the objects behind a trim is `M5.20`/`M5.21`'s. ⚠️ **A partition stamped at the epoch is not judged**, the constraint `M5.86`'s review carried here: a host clock before 1970 stamps `EPOCH`, and treating that as ancient would trim freshly acknowledged records. Retention is `DEFAULT_RETENTION_MS`, Kafka's own 168 hours; per-topic configuration is not read. ⚠️ **The caller re-arms a partition after every commit to it**, by calling `ExpiryHeap::track`: a trimmed partition leaves the heap, and nothing in `MaterializedIndex` notifies, so without that call a partition trimmed once and written again would never expire again. | M5.19 | `trim(new_start_offset)` as the only partition-level retention primitive | Serves FR-33. Advancing the logical start is metadata-only. Acceptance: a test asserting `trim` writes no object and deletes none — deletion is `M5.21`'s lifecycle, reached only once liveness says so — and a test asserting a read below the new start gets `OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE` after a refresh.  ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.19` itself: a new log record, and a refusal where there was a skip.** `MetadataRecord::Trimmed { topic, partition, start }` is an effect folded in log order like a publication or a swap, so a batch holding commits and a trim for one partition folds the same at any page size. It drops index entries *wholly* below the start — an object straddling it still holds live records and stays — and the manifest only when everything it covers is dead. ⚠️ **A trim at or below the current start is a no-op** rather than a refusal, so a retention round re-issuing one after a crash cannot wedge the fold; one **past the end is refused**, because the next produce would land below it, acknowledged and unreadable. ⚠️ **And a read below the start used to be a silent skip**: `find_batches` answered from the first live entry, which moves a consumer past data it never saw on a successful poll. The end-to-end fetch against a trimmed partition is the retention round's to drive, since nothing commits a `Trimmed` until it exists. | done |
| M5.20 | Object liveness: deletable only when **every** partition slice inside it is dead | Serves FR-33, FR-35. ⚠️ **And after `M5.5` this is the normal case, not the exception**: `merge_round` writes one object spanning every partition in a round, so a compacted object is deletable only when every partition inside it has expired — the repacking case below is what compaction itself produces. ⚠️ Otherwise one slow-expiring partition pins a whole object indefinitely — which is what makes repacking a *retention* requirement rather than an efficiency one. Acceptance: a test that an object with 9 dead slices and 1 live one is not deletable, and a test that the same object becomes a compaction candidate for repacking rather than sitting pinned. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.20` itself: liveness is a count the fold keeps, and repacking is split into `M5.89`** (`ADR-0045`). `IndexState` counts the entries naming each object — a commit adds one per staged entry, a swap drops one per retired reference and adds one per installed, a trim drops one per entry it removes — and `MaterializedIndex::references` answers it through the seam, so an object with nine dead slices and one live one answers 1. ⚠️ **A publication releases nothing**: the manifest still names the data objects it absorbed and the fold does not read manifests, so their counts stay up — a storage leak, the direction FR-35 permits. ⚠️ **Zero is the precondition for deletion, not the permission**: a reader holding a reference from before the count fell is covered by the lifecycle's delay (`M5.21`, `M5.22`). Repacking a pinned object is compaction work with its own acceptance and does not stand between M5 and `m5-complete.sh`, so it is its own row. | done |
| M5.21 | Three-state lifecycle — live → logically deleted → deletion queue — with a TTL sweep, idempotent commit, a per-round batch cap **and** backpressure | Serves FR-35. An uncapped queue that grows once creation outruns deletion is a documented pathology in a peer system, so the cap alone is not the answer; backpressure is. ⚠️ **A per-key delete refusal from `oqueue-store` is `Transient` and says nothing about why** (`ADR-0030`): the S3 error code is erased before `classify()` sees it, so "will this key ever delete" is answered from **repetition across sweeps** here, not from a classification the layer below cannot provide. A release can precede the death of the object's last slice — another partition still names it — and a delay counted from the release would then expire while a reader of that slice is still fetching; a sweep's sighting is never earlier than the drop, and costs at most one sweep interval. `Lifecycle` in `oqueue-compact` holds the three states; `DELETE_BATCH_KEYS` (1,000, S3's `DeleteObjects` ceiling) caps a sweep, `DELETION_BACKLOG_KEYS` is the backpressure bound callers read through `admits`, and `QUARANTINE_AFTER_REFUSALS` is 5. ⚠️ **A batch refusal names no key**, so the sweep that meets one retries its keys singly to attribute it. ⚠️ **Nothing calls it yet**: releasing the objects a journaled trim or swap drops is the retention path's end-to-end, which `m5-complete.sh`'s FR-33 leg asserts. | done |

Acceptance: the format round-trips entries and a chain link; entries are ordered by offset and binary-searchable; a manifest naming an object twice is refused on both sides, as `M5.8`'s is; a chain cycle is refused rather than followed; and a manifest at an unknown version is refused by name. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.61` itself: the chain is a link rather than a policy.** The format carries a predecessor key and the parser returns it; *when* to spill — and the rewrite that does it — belongs with the writer that produces manifests, which is `M5.62`'s commit path, so this row ships `PARTITION_MANIFEST_BYTES` and the tests that pin what it is for rather than a spiller with no caller. ⚠️ **And the parser's cursor is now shared** with the composite's: two durable formats reading bytes off the network with the same discipline is one place for a bounds test to be subtly different, so `cursor.rs` holds it and each format passes its own error constructor. | done |
| M5.62 | A partition's history is one manifest reference | Serves NFR-11, FR-34 — `ADR-0042`'s state column. The coordinator holds one reference per partition where it held one entry per `(object, partition)`, which is 86 MB against 225.6 TB at the working set (`M5.73` re-derived both; the row said 40 MB against 97 TB, `ADR-0042`'s inline-width figures). ⚠️ **The tail is untouched** and its 15.1 GB is `M5.10`'s — and `ADR-0043` found it is *not* NFR-11's only remaining half, which `ADR-0042` said: un-absorbed history is the larger term above a 40.2 s sweep. Acceptance: publishing a manifest leaves the partition's history at one entry for any number of objects, asserted for 2 and 64; a rebuild from the log reproduces one entry rather than N; the fold refuses a manifest whose range does not meet the tail's start, because a gap there is records nothing can serve; and `entries()` reflects it. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.62` itself: no trait method, and nothing publishes on the live path.** `MaterializedIndex` is unchanged — an accessor the reader needs is `M5.63`'s, and one with no caller is one no test can distinguish from a wrong one — and no production code emits `ManifestPublished`, so a fetch below a manifest's boundary cannot happen before the reader exists. ⚠️ **And the boundary check is over *offsets*, not tiers**: a publication arriving in the same batch as the commits it covers must see them, because a replay pages the log in arbitrary chunks and a fold that refused such a page could not replay one. | done |
| M5.63 | A history fetch is a manifest read and a ranged GET | Serves FR-13, FR-34 — `ADR-0042`'s read column. GET the partition's manifest, binary-search it for the offset, one ranged GET of the object. ⚠️ **The read count is the claim to test, not the correctness**: the acceptance asserts the count rather than describing it. Acceptance: a fetch over a history range returns the same records as before, byte for byte; the GET count is asserted at 2 cold, 3 across a chain hop, and 1 once the manifest is held; a tail fetch is still one GET (FR-13); and a fetch landing between the manifest's end and the tail's start is answered from whatever holds it rather than by an error. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.63` itself: the counts are asserted where they are a property of the mechanism, not of the fixture.** "2 cold" is a fetch stopping after one batch; the claim that makes this a manifest read rather than a per-object indirection is that a fetch crossing *two* objects under one manifest is 3 and not 4, and that is what the test asserts alongside it. ⚠️ **And "byte for byte" is compared per object, not per response**: the manifest tier and the index tier each contribute a page, so a read crossing the boundary names more batches than it did before — comparing whole responses would assert that the paging did not change rather than that the records did not. | done |
| M5.64 | The manifest-size figures rest on an entry width the format did not have | Serves no FR/NFR — a `minor` from `M5.61`'s passing round. `ADR-0042` priced a manifest entry at 24 B before the format existed; `encode_entry` writes `2 + key + 8 + 4 + 8 + 8`, so ~36 B. The constant's own doc and the ADR's caveat were corrected; the ADR's table cells, the two later quotations of 169 KiB, and `partition_manifest.rs`'s module doc were not. ⚠️ **One of them is load-bearing**: `ADR-0042` says the backlog "lands just over Redpanda's ~128 KiB", and at ~36 B it is ~253 KiB — nearly double, which is a different argument for the same cap. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.64` itself: ~36 B was wrong too, in the same direction.** It is the encoder measured against a four-character *test* key; a real one is `BundleNamer`'s `bundles/{writer}/{sequence:020}` at 51–54 B, so an entry is **84 B** — 30 the format decides plus the key, quoted at the key's wide end because the figure bounds a cold read. The backlog is therefore ~590 KiB, five chain links rather than one, which strengthens the chaining argument instead of softening it. ⚠️ **And the GET count is a derived figure too**, which this row's first round caught still restated: `ADR-0042` quoted doc 14 §3's "1–3 GETs" as the bound, and five links makes a cold fetch of the oldest uncompacted offset six. The ADR now says the 1–3 is the compacted steady state, what the backlog costs, and that shortening the sweep interval is `M5.16`'s lever. Every figure is derived by a test — `an_entry_costs_thirty_bytes_plus_its_object_key`, `the_cap_holds_about_sixteen_hundred_entries` and `an_uncompacted_backlog_is_five_chained_manifests` — each of which seals manifests and subtracts, so the next change to the encoder reds a test rather than leaving a fourth paragraph wrong. Acceptance: every figure derived from the entry width is recomputed from the encoder rather than restated, each site says which it is, and the sentence about Redpanda's cap says what is actually true of the comparison. | done |
| M5.65 | `MAX_MANIFEST_HOPS`'s pin was inserted between a comment and the entry it describes | Serves no FR/NFR — a `minor` from `M5.63`'s passing round, written as a row here because `review.md` rule 15 puts it in the next commit rather than in the one that was reviewed. `check-drift.sh`'s `RUST_BOUNDS` map documents each pinned constant in a comment block above its entry; `M5.63` added `MAX_MANIFEST_HOPS`'s comment and entry *between* the `M10.18a` block and the `BACKOFF_BASE` entry that block describes. Each key now sits under the other's weakening-direction rule and `BACKOFF_BASE` has no comment at all — which is the failure mode the map's own convention exists to prevent, since a pin whose reason belongs to another constant is a pin nobody can check. Acceptance: each entry sits under its own comment, and a case in `tests/gates/negative.sh` plants a pin whose comment block describes a different key and fails. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.65` itself: three rules were written and two were measured worthless.** "The block must *name* its entries" fires on nothing — 33 of the map's 34 blocks describe their constant in prose without spelling it, so the gate went green on the exact arrangement `M5.63` shipped. "The block must not name a *different* pin" fires on seven legitimate cross-references ("bounded by `MIN_SESSION_TIMEOUT_MS`"). A rule about what a comment *means* is not one a grep can hold. ⚠️ **So the rule is positional and the shared case gets a spelling**: every entry sits directly under a comment line, and two pins that genuinely share one decision — `MIN_`/`MAX_SESSION_TIMEOUT_MS`, `MAX_BATCHES_PER_PAGE`/`TAIL_WINDOW_ENTRIES` — say so in a one-line back-reference instead of sitting silently under their neighbour's block. That costs a line and makes "these two are one decision" a claim in the file rather than an inference from whitespace. ⚠️ **And the leg reads `$REPO_ROOT/scripts/check-drift.sh`, not `$0`**: the gate `cd`s to the repo root, so a relative `$0` did not resolve when a review packet invoked it from a scratch tree — every packet reported `check-drift.sh: **FAILED**`, accusing a pin of mis-attribution when none was. A parse that finds no entries now fails rather than printing `ok` with a count taken from the shell array. | done |
| M5.66 | An empty manifest resolution is a success, and a client re-polls forever | Serves FR-13 — a `minor` from `M5.63`'s passing round, and one that becomes real the moment something publishes a manifest. `Cluster::manifest_batches` answers an offset older than every link of the chain with `Ok(vec![])`, and `read/manifest.rs`'s own doc calls that "the reaped case, which the caller answers as it answers an object the store no longer has" — which is false: `fetch/partition.rs` maps only `Error::ObjectNotFound` to `OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE`, so the client gets an empty partition with error code 0 and re-polls the same offset. That is hazard H4's shape on a new tier — a successful poll returning nothing while the records are gone for good. ⚠️ **Unreachable today and scheduled anyway**: `M5.62` recorded that no production code emits `ManifestPublished`, and `M5.13` is the commit path that will. Acceptance: an offset below every link of the chain is refused rather than answered empty, the caller maps it to `OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE`, and a test asserts the client-visible code rather than the batch count — plus the doc says which of the two an empty resolution is. | todo |
| M5.67 | Nine of the packet's gates have never run against a staged tree | Serves no FR/NFR — found by `M5.55` the moment the packet stopped conflating a skip with a pass. `run_gates_on_staged_tree` materialises the staged bytes with `git checkout-index` and plants a `.git` **file** so no gate can read the real tree — and a gate that then finds no tracked files `skip`s and exits zero. So `check-backlog-rows`, `check-core-contract`, `check-drift`, `check-file-size`, `check-sans-io`, `check-secrets`, `check-tests-kept`, `check-unsafe` and `check-budget` have been reported to every reviewer as passed while running none of their own checks. ⚠️ **Nine, and the tenth is the measurement's own lesson**: `check-conformance-matrix` was in this list until `M5.55`'s first round found the classifier's `ok` anchor missing `lib.sh`'s two leading spaces — it reaches and passes two of its own checks and skips only the `git grep` leg. A count taken from a broken instrument is a count to re-take. ⚠️ **The commit hook does run them**, so nothing reached history unchecked — what was wrong is what the *packet* told a reviewer, which is where attention gets spent. Acceptance: the staged tree is a repository the gates can read — `git init` plus an index, and a HEAD for the two that diff against one — so each gate either runs or says which environment it needs; a `tests/harness/review-packet.sh` case asserts a git-reading gate reaches its own check rather than skipping; and the count of gates reported `not run here` for a reason other than a missing toolchain is zero. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.67` itself, twice.** `check-budget.sh` joins `GATES_EXCLUDED`: its input is `target/timings/suite.tsv`, which `target/` keeps out of every materialised tree, so it could only ever report itself unrun — and a permanently unrun row trains the same blindness a permanently red one does. And the remaining two, `check-core-contract` and `check-tests-kept`, answer about *this* diff ("no .rs files staged") rather than about the environment, which is the gate working rather than skipping. ⚠️ **And a failure to build the repository must put the barrier back.** `$tree` lives under `target/`, inside the repository under review, so a scratch tree with no `.git` of its own has git walk up and find the real one — every gate would then check the working tree while looking green. The `.git` file is restored on that path, which is why it still exists. ⚠️ **And every `git` call here runs with the caller's git environment removed**, which the first round measured rather than argued: with `GIT_INDEX_FILE` inherited, `add -A` writes the scratch tree's entries into the **real** index pointing at blobs in the scratch object store, and the cleanup trap then deletes those objects — the change under review destroyed, with a zero exit status the failure branch never sees. | done |
| M5.69 | A `Cargo.toml` that is a directory reads as a workspace without the crate | Serves FR-34 — a `minor` from `M5.58`'s passing third round, and the fifth instance of that row's own failure mode. `check-sans-io.sh`'s `workspace_claims` answers 1 ("not claimed") when `os.path.isfile("Cargo.toml")` is false, which is true of a `Cargo.toml` that is a **directory** or a dangling symlink — neither of which is a workspace without that crate, and both of which are "could not tell". The whole leg then skips a violating tree. ⚠️ **One line**, and it is a row rather than a fourth round because `review.md` rule 15 forbids opening a round for a minor and round three was the cap. Acceptance: `exists` decides whether to answer 1 or 2, so a path that is present but unreadable as a file is a 2; and `negative.sh` carries a tree whose `Cargo.toml` is a directory. | todo |
| M5.70 | Nothing catches a merge-conflict marker in a tracked file | Serves no FR/NFR — found by `M5.65`'s second round, which read twelve conflict markers in the *staged* `tests/gates/negative.sh`. `bash -n` on those bytes exits 2, so the whole suite failed to parse and **zero of 175 cases ran** — and the pre-commit suite was green, because no gate lints or executes that file and `check-crate.sh` covers Rust only. ⚠️ **The commit would have landed a test suite that runs nothing**, which is the silent-success shape `negative.sh` itself exists to catch, in `negative.sh` itself. ⚠️ **A `.rs` file would have been caught** by `cargo fmt`; shell, Markdown and TOML have no such reader. Acceptance: a gate refuses any tracked file containing a conflict marker at line start, with the file and line named; `tests/gates/negative.sh` carries a tree with one; and every shell script this repository tracks is `bash -n`-parsed, since a suite that cannot parse is a suite that proves nothing. ⚠️ **Amended by `M5.70` itself: both legs read the *index*, not the working tree**, because the bytes that land in history are the staged ones and a gate reading the disk would pass a tree whose staged version is broken. ⚠️ **And the `=======` arm is length-exact**: a Markdown setext heading underlines with `=`, this repository's docs use them, and a gate refusing every `===` line would be unusable here — so `negative.sh` carries a converse case for it alongside the three failing ones. ⚠️ **And the first round found the amendment's own claim false in the parse leg**: a `[[ -f "$f" ]]` guard made it skip a script deleted from the working tree but still staged — the bytes that land in history — and print a count larger than the number it had checked. The guard is gone and a case plants that tree. ⚠️ **The parse diagnostic is captured, not spooled to `/tmp`**: `build.md` rule 19 aside, anything in the way of that path makes the redirection fail, the failure branch fire, and a good script be reported unparsable — a gate blocking every commit for a reason unrelated to the tree. | done |
| M5.68 | The list exemption's module branch is covered by nothing | Serves no FR/NFR — a `minor` from `M5.56`'s passing round, and pre-existing: the fixture `M5.56` replaced never reached this branch either. `list_exemption_holds` refuses a list file that declares a module, and replacing that guard with `if false` leaves `tests/gates/negative.sh` wholly green — because every one of the ten fixtures plants a *second item*, so the `items != 1` leg fails first and the module leg is unreachable from all of them, including the two that plant `pub mod inner;`. The failure it is written against: an `error.rs` reduced to a single `pub mod codes;` at 600 lines keeps its `list` exemption and the gate exits 0, which is exactly "the file stopped being a list" the exemption exists to catch. Acceptance: a fixture whose *only* top-level item is a module declaration, so the count leg passes and the module leg is what fails; and replacing the module guard with `if false` reds that case and no other. | todo |

Killed with two new tests: a follower heartbeats at the halfway point of its own session timeout, then the group is shown still Stable one second past the *original* deadline but short of the *renewed* one (kills both the no-op and the sign-flip); and a member's own deadline reached at *exactly* the sweep instant (no more, no less, under paused time's own deterministic advancement) is shown evicted, not kept one sweep longer (kills the `>=` mutant). The reviewer judged deferral inadequate and empirically reproduced the real consequence: a survivor's *every* subsequent `JoinGroup` for that group is refused `INCONSISTENT_GROUP_PROTOCOL`, permanently (four consecutive attempts, all refused) -- not a wrong error code for one call, but an unrecoverable group outage from the single most ordinary event this feature exists to handle (one member of a >1-member group timing out). Fixed in `join_group::round::open_round` itself: a `PreparingRebalance` state with no locally-open round now starts collecting rather than refusing -- the round genuinely is open, just not tracked here yet, so no event is re-fired (there is no legal `(PreparingRebalance, Join)` transition to fire in the first place). Two regression tests reproduce the reviewer's own repro and were confirmed to fail without the fix, then pass with it restored: `join_group::round::tests::a_group_moved_to_preparing_rebalance_by_an_external_actor_still_accepts_a_join` (a focused unit test driving the coordinator to `PreparingRebalance` directly, bypassing `GroupJoins::join` entirely) and `heartbeat::tests::a_survivor_can_rejoin_after_an_eviction_the_group_is_not_permanently_wedged` (the full cross-module path: evict, then rejoin through the real handler). The module doc's own framing was corrected to describe the fix rather than a deferral, and a second, narrower race the reviewer traced but did not independently reproduce (`sweep`'s own `AllMembersGone` decision uses this module's own tracked-membership count as a proxy for "the group is truly empty," which a fresh, not-yet-registered `JoinGroup` round can make wrong) is named honestly as a remaining, unfixed risk rather than silently carried forward. | done |

Committed offsets survive a coordinator restart — `M4.2`'s `GroupCoordinator` seam persists through the same durability mechanism `oqueue_coordinator::Coordinator` already uses for metadata, not a second bespoke store. Acceptance: a fault-injection test (`M10`'s own harness) killing the coordinator after a commit and before an ack is impossible by construction (the ack IS the durable write, `ADR-0020`'s own "one flush, one PUT" instinct applied here), and a restart test asserting every previously-committed offset replays intact. ⚠️ **Built.** New `ADR-0035` decides the open question `ADR-0034` (`M4.2`) deliberately left standing: committed offsets get their own `GroupMetadataLog` seam in `oqueue-core` — `MetadataLog`'s own shape verbatim (`append`/`read_from`/`last_version`, the same five durability guarantees), its own small exhaustive `GroupMetadataRecord` (one variant: `OffsetCommitted{group, topic, partition, offset}`), and its own `FakeGroupMetadataLog` — rather than a new `MetadataRecord` variant routed through `oqueue_coordinator::Coordinator`. The ADR's own three reasons: `MetadataEntry` is monomorphic in `MetadataRecord`, not generic; `Coordinator::commit` is hard-wired to `(ObjectKey, Vec<CommittedSpan>)`, not generic over record kind; and `GroupCoordinator` is already an independent seam from `MaterializedIndex` by the same design, one level up. "Not a second bespoke store" is read as ruling out a hand-rolled persistence format, not as requiring literal reuse of one running `Coordinator` instance across two unrelated domains. New `FaultGroupMetadataLog<L>` (`refuse_append` only, `FaultMetadataLog`'s own decorator shape, not made generic over it — two small traits, no shared code, an explicit ADR consequence rather than an early, unproven generalization over two data points). `CommittedOffsets` (`M4.12`) gained a `log: Arc<dyn GroupMetadataLog>` field, an `async fn open(log)` replacing its old `Default` (replays every entry via a paged `read_from` loop honoring guarantee 5 — a short page means done, not "fewer this time"), and its own `commit` became `async`: durable append *before* the in-memory map updates, `ADR-0020`'s own "the ack IS the durable write" instinct — the response this handler builds cannot be constructed before the corresponding `append` future resolves `Ok`, because nothing in the module has anything to construct one from before then. Versions are assigned optimistically (read `last_version`, try to append there, retry up to `MAX_COMMIT_RETRIES` on a losing race) rather than serialized through a held lock — `async-concurrency.md` rules 6 and 8 both rule out holding a lock across the `.await` or using one to sequence steps; the log's own `NonMonotonicCommitVersion` validation is the real serialization point. `offset_commit.rs`'s own `handle`/`commit_topic` became `async`; `dispatch.rs`'s own `offset_commit_handle` gained the matching `.await`. A durable-append failure answers `UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR` per partition, `join_group.rs`'s own precedent for an internal/storage failure that is not the client's own mistake. `Cluster::new` became `async` (`ADR-0035`'s own "no hook into `Coordinator::open`" decision: opening the group log is its own step, done inside `Cluster::new` rather than folded into the topic log's own bootstrap) — both real call sites (`bin/oqueue`'s composition root, `testing.rs`'s own fixture builder) were already inside async functions, so this cost one `.await` each, not a signature cascade. `testing.rs`'s `Fixture` gained a fault-capable `group_metadata_log` by default, `TestStore`'s own "capable by default, not on request" precedent, plus `refuse_group_metadata_append`/`heal_group_metadata_log` convenience methods. Nineteen tests: the fault-injection acceptance criterion itself (a refused append leaves nothing committed and answers `UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR`, not a success — verified load-bearing by temporarily letting a refused append answer `NONE` and watching the test catch it before restoring), the restart-replay acceptance criterion itself (a second `CommittedOffsets::open` against the identical log sees every offset the first one committed, the same "same log, fresh in-memory state" shape an actual process restart would present, `FakeGroupMetadataLog`'s own not-yet-durable-across-a-real-restart status named honestly rather than overclaimed), and two pagination tests proving the replay loop correctly continues past a full page and correctly stops after a trailing short page rather than assuming one `read_from` call sees everything — plus the nine tests from `M4.12`/`M4.13` updated for the new `async` signatures, all still green. ⚠️ **The first gate run against this diff found eleven surviving mutants, all inside `oqueue-core`'s two new files** — `FakeGroupMetadataLog`'s own `len`/`is_empty`/`Debug`/`validate`'s exact `<=` boundary/`read_from`'s exact `>=` boundary, and `FaultGroupMetadataLog::refuse_append`/`heal`, none of which `CommittedOffsets`'s own indirect tests constrained tightly enough. Fixed by adding six direct unit tests for the two new `oqueue-core` types themselves rather than continuing to rely on exercising them only through their caller — the same lesson `FakeMetadataLog`'s own untested-but-thoroughly-indirectly-exercised precedent does not transfer to a type with no equivalent conformance suite yet. The twelfth survivor, `CommittedOffsets::open`'s own pagination boundary (`got < REPLAY_PAGE_SIZE`, mutated to `>`), turned out to be invisible to any test observing final replayed state alone — the mutation costs one extra, empty `read_from` round trip past the log's own end, not a wrong answer — so `FakeGroupMetadataLog` gained a `read_from_calls()` counter (`Cluster::topic_lookups`'s own shape) and the new trailing-short-page test asserts the exact call count, which is a real property worth pinning regardless of the mutant: a caller replaying this log against a real, billed object-storage engine should not pay for a page it didn't need. That counter's own two mutations (`read_from_calls` replaced with a fixed `0` or `1`) surfaced on the next gate run — exercised only indirectly, from `oqueue-broker`'s own separate test binary, which `check-mutants.sh`'s per-crate scoping cannot see — and were killed with one more direct unit test in `oqueue-core` itself, incrementing the counter three times and asserting three, not a number either fixed mutation could satisfy. All thirteen survivors across both gate runs killed by tests, none argued away in `baselines/mutants.txt`; every new/strengthened test was verified load-bearing by applying its exact mutation, confirming the predicted failure, and restoring. `check-drift.sh` gained two `RUST_BOUNDS` entries (`REPLAY_PAGE_SIZE`, `MAX_COMMIT_RETRIES`, both genuine thresholds with their own weakening direction recorded); `check-core-contract.sh`/`check-sans-io.sh`/`check-fencing-seam.sh`/`check-file-size.sh`/`check-unsafe.sh` all pass. ⚠️ **Round 1 review (changes-requested, 1 major, 2 minor, all fixed):** (1) `commit`'s post-append step and a racing commit's own post-append step for the *same* key were not ordered relative to each other, even though the log's own `NonMonotonicCommitVersion` check orders the appends themselves — `connection.rs` spawns every request as its own task, so two pipelined commits to one `(group, topic, partition)` can append in one order and then run their own `offsets.insert` in the other, letting the causally earlier write clobber the later one in the in-memory map `OffsetFetch` reads, contradicting the module's own "last write wins" claim. Fixed: the map now stores `(CommitVersion, i64)` per key, `apply` (the one function both `commit`'s post-append step and `open`'s replay step now call, rather than `commit` inserting directly) accepts a write only if no version is stored yet or the stored one is older, so whichever call's version is durably later always wins regardless of which call's own insert happens to run last. A new direct unit test (`a_later_committed_version_is_never_overwritten_by_an_earlier_one_applied_after_it`) applies the later version first and the earlier one second — the exact interleaving the race produces — and was confirmed to fail with the earlier value winning before the fix, by temporarily reverting `apply`'s guard to an unconditional overwrite. (2) `MAX_COMMIT_RETRIES`'s own doc cited `security.md` rule 3 (`no panic! reachable from client bytes`), unrelated to bounding a retry loop — corrected to rule 13 (resource exhaustion). (3) `Cluster` holds one `GroupMetadataLog` shared by every group, so contention on this constant is cluster-wide, not per-key — named explicitly in the constant's own doc as a known, unscheduled limitation rather than solved now (fixing it means either partitioning the log or building backoff, neither of which this task's own acceptance criterion asked for). | done |

| M4.16 | `ownedPartitions` round-tripped so `cooperative-sticky` clients work | Serves FR-20. ⚠️ The invariant is that a partition is revoked by its previous owner before being handed to a new one, which is why cooperative rebalancing takes two rounds; mixed-protocol groups are unsafe and this task does not attempt to make them safe. Two consumers never converged and both consumed the same partitions in between: FR-20's invariant failing with no mixed protocols in sight. A round now waits for the *roster* it had (`OpenRound::awaiting`), so a newcomer cannot close one on its own. | done |

Acceptance: the harness drives real `librdkafka` and Java consumer instances through an initial join, a consumer added, and a consumer removed, asserting after each that the group's partitions are spread across the live members with no partition owned by two at once; a skip, not a silent pass, when a client is unavailable. ⚠️ **Three single-partition topics, not one multi-partition topic**: `Cluster::ensure_topic` hardcodes `partitions: 1` and no `CreateTopics` is dispatched, so a partition count is not something a client can ask for and one topic would only ever prove one consumer got it. ⚠️ **A real broker defect came out of writing this, invisible to 280 unit tests**: the `SyncGroup` assignment barrier held no generation, so a follower syncing for generation N that arrived before its leader was answered from generation N-1's map — and for a consumer that joined during N-1 that map holds its own *empty* slice, so it concluded it owned nothing, went `steady`, and stayed idle while the incumbents kept every partition. Adding a consumer to a working group simply did not work. The barrier now carries its generation and is a `Mutex<Option<_>>` with one durable `Notify` per group rather than a rotated `OnceLock`, which also closes the lost-wakeup the old code documented as \"abandoned to its own deadline\" — and `wait_for_assignment` now registers on the `Notify` before it looks, since `notified()` only registers when first polled and checking first left a submission in that window unheard. ⚠️ **A second divergence was found alongside it and fixed, but it is not what caused the starvation**, and review verified that: the member that opens a round enrols first, so `elect`'s `members.first()` made the newest consumer leader of every group it joined and moved the leader on every rebalance. Kafka's membership is join-ordered and its leader is the longest-standing member, which a sticky assignor is entitled to assume; `finalize_close` now orders each round's members by their position in the previous roster. The client harness passes with that ordering removed, so it is pinned by unit tests rather than by client evidence, and this row says so rather than claiming a symptom it does not demonstrate. ⚠️ **FR-21's restart leg is reported, not asserted, and this row was narrowed to say so** (`sdd.md`'s \"when the spec turns out to be wrong\"; the row was `todo`, so the freeze does not bind it). Measured: committed offset 5 before a broker restart, `-1001` after. `serve` wires `FakeGroupMetadataLog`, an in-memory `Vec`, so no offset can survive a process restart — a recorded deferral (`ADR-0035`, and `roadmap.md`'s deferred table receives the durable engine in `M6`), which `serve` itself warns about at startup. `offset_survival.py` measures it and the harness reports a **skip** naming that reason, never a pass, so a green harness cannot be read as FR-21 verified — and **fails** if the offsets ever do survive, so `M6` landing cannot pass unnoticed either. `M4.23` must not claim FR-21's restart test.  ⚠️ **One unrelated fix, taken because it failed this commit's own gate** and `AGENTS.md` forbids committing a tree known to be broken: `Cluster::wait_until_replayed` bounded itself by a *yield count* (`MAX_REPLAY_WAIT_YIELDS`, 10_000), which is no bound in time on a `multi_thread` runtime — yielding reschedules the calling task, so under CPU saturation ten thousand of them elapse in milliseconds without the replay task ever being scheduled. That is why `dispatch::tests::api_versions_round_trips_through_a_connection` failed intermittently on the gate (and under `cargo-mutants`) while passing 300 consecutive runs in isolation; `M4.16`'s commit body recorded it as an unexplained flake, and this is the explanation. Now `MAX_REPLAY_WAIT_POLLS` (2_000) sleeps of `REPLAY_WAIT_POLL` (1 ms), a real ~2 s bound, both pinned in `check-drift.sh`. Measured under CPU saturation: **8 of 25 failures before, 0 of 25 after**. ⚠️ Still correct under `start_paused = true` — tokio auto-advances a paused clock only once every task is idle, so a runnable replay task is polled before the timer fires. ⚠️ **The ceiling is 2 s rather than 10 s because of what it costs `check-mutants` in wall clock**: every mutant that stalls replay waits the whole bound out, which at 10 s took that gate from ~40 s to ~93 s; at 2 s it measures ~72 s, so the cost is reduced rather than removed. ⚠️ **It is *not* an NFR-56 failure, and a first draft of this row claimed it was** — caught by review, and `M4.21`'s row three rows above had already recorded the correct fact. `check-budget.sh` removes every gate over `COMPILING_GATE_MS` (5 s) from the total it judges, so `check-mutants` is invisible to that gate at 40 s, 72 s or 93 s alike. The budget failure seen while choosing this constant was the **warm** remainder at 10113 ms against a 10000 ms budget — 113 ms of ordinary erosion, which would have happened at either ceiling. The distinction matters because the false version would tell a future agent that restoring a longer bound breaches a budget non-negotiable 2 forbids relieving, and so leave a real false-failure unfixed; it is a wall-clock trade and nothing more. ⚠️ Lowering the count is not a threshold weakening: the unit changed, and the bound went from unbounded-in-yields to a real 2 s. | done |
