| M4.20 | The `brevity` skill, and the two review adapters that load it | Serves NFR-56 from the other side: `M4.19` and `M4.21` cut what the gates cost in wall clock, this cuts what a turn costs in tokens. Every reply and every review finding this project produces is written by an agent with no length discipline of its own, and the wrapper — preamble, a recap of the diff it was just handed, a narration line before each tool call, a closing summary — is pure cost that no reader uses. ⚠️ **It cuts the wrapper and never the content**, which is the whole design and the reason the skill is long enough to need a body: a "be brief" instruction with no `Never cut` list produces an agent that drops a negation, abbreviates a symbol name, or concedes a correction to save a sentence. So the skill names what is never compressible — code, exact error strings, numbers and units, `not`/`never`/`only`/`except`, and any caveat that changes what the reader would do — and names the cases that are written at full length regardless, of which **correcting a false premise** is the one that matters most here: brevity pressure pushes a model to agree rather than argue, and a reviewer that concedes is worth nothing. ⚠️ **Fake compression is banned separately**, because it is the failure mode an instruction to be brief actually produces: invented abbreviations (`cfg`, `impl`, `fn`) tokenize the same as the full word, an arrow standing in for a word is its own token, and dropped articles cost the reader while saving nothing. ⚠️ **Out of scope by design**: code, comments, commit messages, PR bodies, docs and memory files stay ordinary prose — this row is itself written under that exemption. `.claude/agents/reviewer.md` and `.claude/agents/milestone-reviewer.md` gain a pointer to the skill and nothing else, keeping `AGENTS.md`'s rule that `.claude/` holds no procedures; both say explicitly that brevity never overrides the finding format, so `file:line`, the severity and the concrete failure scenario survive in full. ⚠️ **Why this is a task rather than a loose file**: an untracked `SKILL.md` makes `AGENTS.md`'s generated skills region stale the moment it exists, so `build-index-check` fails on every commit until the skill is committed — which is how it surfaced, blocking `M4.21`'s gate. ⚠️ **The generated row's wording lives in the frontmatter, not in the table.** `build-index.sh` takes the first sentence of `description:`, so the authored wording had to move into the skill and the table be regenerated from it; hand-editing the table would go stale on the next rebuild. `.agents/skills/README.md`'s own table is authored rather than generated and is updated by hand, as its neighbours are. | done |

| M4.61 | A harness ceiling that fires leaves the leg's own broker running | Serves FR-20, FR-4 — filed by `M4.53`, `review.md` rule 15. `run_bounded` signals the direct child only, which its own header records as the first of three limits `timeout(1)` does not have. `M4.53` made that limit reachable: three of the legs it bounds — `idempotent_conformance.py`, `tls_sasl.py` (its own broker, for the certificate's sake) and `offset_survival.py` (a broker it starts, kills and restarts) — leave a broker running when the ceiling fires, and `kafka-client-harness.sh`'s EXIT trap covers only `$BROKER_PID`, the one it started itself. ⚠️ **The frame-dropping proxy is *not* one of them**, which a first version of this row claimed: it is an `asyncio.start_server` inside the same interpreter `run_bounded` signals, so it dies with the child. Review caught it, and the cost of the wrong claim is precise — whoever implements this writes a reaper for a process that does not exist. ⚠️ **The leak is on the failure path, which is where it is least likely to be noticed**: the gate has already gone red. ⚠️ **It does not hold a port** — all three brokers bind `127.0.0.1:0`, so the next run's failure mode is accumulated processes and memory, not a bind conflict; the same review corrected that too. ⚠️ **Not fixed inside `run_bounded`**: killing a process group needs `set -m` and a negative pid, which changes job-control behaviour for every gate that sources `lib.sh`. The cheaper repair is in the scripts — each already owns the subprocess it starts and can reap it from a `finally` or an `atexit`, which also covers the case `run_bounded` cannot see at all: the script dying on its own deadline. The re-raise semantics are defensible; the sentence over-reaches, and whichever way this row resolves it must say which. ⚠️ Second: `_run_bounded_stop` sends `SIGKILL` unconditionally after a poll loop that has just observed the pid gone, so it knowingly signals a pid it saw exit — the pid-reuse hazard `run_bounded`'s own header records, in code whose loop condition already holds the answer. | M4.65 | A same-generation refusal is overwritten by the leader's own assignment | Serves FR-20 — filed by `M4.64`'s protocol lens. ⚠️ **Not FR-22**, which `ADR-0033`/`M4.24` deferred and which eleven frozen rows still cite wrongly (`M4.70`). `sync_group::submit_assignment` computes `synced` from the record the transition returned and never re-reads it, and `barrier::submit`'s guard is `a.generation > generation`, so a same-generation write is permitted — while `refuse`'s mirror-image guard (`a.generation == generation && a.map.is_some()`) refuses exactly that. A `MemberLeft` landing between the transition and the submit is legal from `Stable`: it takes the group to `PreparingRebalance@N` and publishes `{N, None}`, and the leader's task then resumes with a stale `synced` and overwrites it with `{N, Some(map)}`. Followers just told to rejoin read `Known::Mine` instead and are answered `NONE` with a slice for a generation the group has left — the revoke-before-reassign harm `M4.42`/`M4.45` exist to prevent, arriving through the writer `M4.47` added. Acceptance: the submission re-reads the record under the barrier's own lock; a test drives the interleaving with `crate::testing::poll_once` and asserts the follower reads `Known::Refused`, and fails against the guard as it stands. ⚠️ **"The two guards are symmetric" was the other half of this criterion and it is wrong**, which `M4.64`'s round-two review recorded and building it confirmed: giving `submit` the mirror of `refuse`'s guard refuses a leader retrying after a transient append failure, because `{generation, None}` is also what that leader's own first attempt published — `durability::the_same_leader_succeeds_once_the_log_heals` turns red. Only the coordinator's record separates the two. ⚠️ **Built.** `barrier::submit` takes a fourth argument, `still_at_this_generation: impl FnOnce() -> bool`, called while holding the cell's lock; `sync_group::submit_assignment` passes a re-read of the record. A re-read *before* the call would not have closed it — the two statements are synchronous, so nothing on this runtime thread interleaves, but the transitions actor is its own task on its own thread. Asking under the lock puts the question on the same side as `refuse`'s write, so whichever writer takes the lock first settles the generation, which is the semantics `heartbeat.rs:318-322` already claims when it calls `refuse` on every removal. Lock order is cell-then-record and is the only order in the crate (`async-concurrency.md` rule 9): every `refuse` caller releases what it holds first, and nothing the coordinator does reaches back. Two tests off one helper that drives the interleaving by hand — `a_leader_that_resumes_after_the_group_left_does_not_overwrite_the_refusal` (the leader is answered `REBALANCE_IN_PROGRESS`, the cell still reads `Known::Refused`) and `a_follower_told_to_rejoin_is_not_then_handed_that_generations_slice`; both observed red at `left: 0, right: 27` with the closure stubbed to return `true` unconditionally. `sync_group.rs`'s own comment claiming the `Ok` arm "needs no second read and no second race" is corrected where it stands, since that sentence named the absent race this row found; `is_stable_at` holds the question both readings ask. ⚠️ **Round 1 review (changes-requested, 1 blocking, 3 minors, all fixed): the fix opened a second stranding route.** `submit` now returns `None` for two reasons, and the arm answering it issued no refusal — right for the older reason, where every follower already reads `Known::Superseded`, and wrong for the new one: a newcomer joining a group that has reached `Stable` plans `GroupEvent::Join`, not `MemberJoinedDuringSync`, so `join_group::round` publishes nothing and the cell holds nothing for the generation the leader was submitting for. Measured by the reviewer at `waited_ms=3000000` — the exact stranding `M4.43` and `M4.47` exist to end, arriving through the repair for a different one, which is this milestone's own recurring shape landing on its own fix. The arm now calls `refuse` unconditionally (a no-op for the older reason, whose guard declines a later generation — the old comment's stated reason for having no call was itself wrong about `refuse`), and `a_follower_is_woken_when_the_leader_is_refused_by_a_route_that_published_nothing` pins it, observed red without the call. The three minors were all false claims this change wrote: "the tests below hold no coordinator" (`parked.rs`'s fixture holds one; the true statement is that these call sites consult none), "after it has read the record" (the record arrives *with* the oneshot, which is the whole race), and a lock-order paragraph arguing the right conclusion from the wrong locks and not saying that the signature enforces nothing. | done |
| M4.66 | Nothing bounds the sync phase by the number the join phase was bounded by | Serves FR-20 — filed by `M4.64`'s protocol lens. `join_group::deadline::barrier_ms` clamps the client's own `rebalance_timeout_ms` to at most `MAX_BARRIER_MS`, so a member asking 60 s waits 60 s; `sync_group::deadline::MAX_SYNC_WAIT_MS` is a flat `3_000_000` derived from no client value at all, because `SyncGroupRequest` carries no timeout field. Its own doc argues the two are "chosen equal" and that a real client's `rebalance.timeout.ms` "already bounds the whole join-then-sync round trip … so this alone is never the tighter limit" — false in the direction that matters: the reference consumer's default is `300_000`, so the sync ceiling is ten times looser than the number the join half honours, and a follower no wake reaches waits fifty minutes. `waited_ms=3000000` is the exact stranding `M4.47` proved. Acceptance: the sync wait is derived from the same value the join barrier was, or the doc drops the "never the tighter limit" claim and says why a fixed ceiling is right; either way a test pins what the follower's deadline is computed from. ⚠️ **Derived, and the alternative was disproved rather than declined.** The fixed ceiling rests on something else bounding the phase, and nothing does: `reopened.rs`'s own note already records that a parked follower is not heartbeating — both reference clients disable the heartbeat thread for the duration of a rebalance — so `Heartbeats::sweep`, which is request-driven with no background reaper, never runs on its behalf. Real Kafka bounds the same phase the same way, re-arming each member's expiration on the group's `rebalanceTimeoutMs` rather than its `sessionTimeoutMs` once the join completes. ⚠️ **Built.** `sync_group::deadline::sync_wait_ms(Option<Duration>) -> u64` mirrors `join_group::deadline::barrier_ms`, clamped by the same `MAX_SYNC_WAIT_MS = 3_000_000`, which stays a ceiling on the group's number rather than the number. `SyncGroups::Entry` gains `rebalance_timeout`, written by `join_group::round::apply_open` (outside its `is_ok` guard: a refused transition leaves the group on a round somebody already opened) and read by `sync_group::handle`; `None` — a group no round opened — falls back to the ceiling, which is every prior caller's behaviour. Two tests, one per half, because a test of the reader alone passes against a broker where nothing ever writes the value: `a_round_opened_by_a_real_join_records_what_it_was_opened_with` drives the real `JoinGroup` handler, and `a_followers_wait_is_its_groups_own_number_not_the_ceiling` asserts the *elapsed* time (45 s asked, under 60 s answered) rather than the code, since `REBALANCE_IN_PROGRESS` is what the ceiling already answers and asserting it alone is the vacuity `M4.58`'s row records. Both observed red — `left: None right: Some(30s)`, and `3000s` — with each half removed in turn, plus three unit tests on `sync_wait_ms`. Two false docs corrected where they stand: `MAX_SYNC_WAIT_MS`'s "chosen equal ... so this alone is never the tighter limit", and `wait_for_assignment`'s deferral to "a later task (`M4.9`/`M4.11`)" — both of which closed without taking it, so the deferral had no receiver. ⚠️ **Round 1 review (changes-requested, 1 blocking, 2 majors, 1 minor, all fixed): deriving a wait needs a floor, and a group's number is not one member's.** The blocking finding was measured end to end — a `JoinGroup` with `rebalance_timeout_ms=0` (legal, and what `barrier_ms` clamps to zero) made a *different* member's follower answer `REBALANCE_IN_PROGRESS` at `waited = 0ns`, handed a rejoin instead of the slice a leader submitted a millisecond later. `barrier_ms` needs no floor because a zero there shortens only the asking member's own round; this phase is where the same zero reaches everyone. `sync_wait_ms` now clamps into `[MIN_SYNC_WAIT_MS, MAX_SYNC_WAIT_MS]`, and `MIN_SYNC_WAIT_MS` is `heartbeat::deadline::MIN_SESSION_TIMEOUT_MS` rather than a second opinion on the same question. First major: the writer was last-writer-wins, so whichever member opened the round set the bound for everyone — an application may legitimately run `max.poll.interval.ms=1000`, and that member would refuse followers before a leader's `SyncComplete` append could land, re-opening the round they were refused into. It now folds the maximum, monotonic over the group's life on purpose: a fold that only lengthens is bounded by the ceiling, which is the behaviour it replaced. Second major: the write sat in `apply_open` under a comment claiming it was "the group's rather than this attempt's" while passing this attempt's argument, and a member joining a round somebody else opened never reached it — moved to the top of `GroupJoins::join`, before the rounds lock, so every joining member records and no lock is nested. Minor: the reader used `entry(..).or_default()`, inserting on every follower's request, harmless only because `entry_for` inserts one line earlier in `handle`. Two more tests, both observed red — `left: Some(1s) right: Some(45s)` and `waited: 0ns`. ⚠️ **Round 2 review (`pass`, 2 majors, 3 minors, all fixed): the round-1 repair for one major was wrong in the load-bearing direction.** Recording every *attempt* rather than every admitted member meant a join refused for an unusable protocol while asking `rebalance_timeout_ms=3_000_000` left the group at the ceiling for the rest of the process — `waited_ms=3000000`, the `M4.47` stranding this row exists to end, set by a member that never joined. The comment arguing it ("a refused join cannot shorten anyone's wait, only lengthen it, so nothing is bought") named lengthening as harmless when lengthening to the ceiling *is* the defect. The call is now gated on enrolment — `JoinOutcome::Ready` or `Pending`, since `Refused`'s own doc is "this member was never enrolled" and a first join with an empty `member_id` is `Pending` rather than `Ready`. Second major: the placement in `join`'s `Step::Done` arm was unconstrained — review measured that moving the call back to `apply_open`, the placement round 1 rejected, left the suite green, because every test drove one member and that member is always the round-*opening* one. Two more tests, each observed red against the defect it names: `a_refused_join_does_not_set_the_groups_number` (`left: Some(3000s) right: Some(30s)`) and `a_member_joining_an_open_round_raises_the_groups_number` (`left: Some(6s) right: Some(300s)`), both driving real `JoinGroup` handlers on spawned tasks because a single poll stops before the recording step and awaiting to completion closes the round. Three minors, fixed with them because the hash was changing regardless: two docs this change wrote that the floor had already falsified, and `M4.72` bucketed with deliverable repairs when its own row is bookkeeping. ⚠️ **Monotonicity is a stated limitation, not a claim**: the fold never resets, so a member that legitimately asked for fifty minutes holds the group there after leaving, where real Kafka recomputes per round — bounded by the ceiling either way, and a resettable fold needs the barrier lock taken inside the rounds lock. ⚠️ **Two gates `check-crate.sh` does not run caught the rest**, which is why the commit hook is the commit path: `check-drift` refused `MIN_SYNC_WAIT_MS` as an unpinned threshold, and it could not be pinned while it was written as an expression over the sibling constant — non-negotiable 2 pins a literal, so it is a literal with `const _: () = assert!(..)` holding the tie, which fails to compile if the session floor moves without a decision about this one. `check-file-size` refused `reopened.rs` at 515 lines; the `JoinGroup` helpers moved beside `seat` and `sync` in `tests.rs`, where `M4.66`'s second caller had been reaching for them through `super::reopened::` anyway. | done |

A `Metadata` request with no topics named is real Kafka's own "every topic" sentinel — through `M9.9`'s index that must mean "every topic this principal can see," not "every topic in the system," or `M9.8`'s whole point is undone through the one path most likely to go untested. ⚠️ **Silent omission, not an error code** — `M9.1`'s verified finding: real Kafka's own null-topic-array path never reports an unauthorized topic at all (`unauthorizedForDescribeTopicMetadata` is `Set.empty` for this case specifically), "so we've not even checked if they exist or not." `M9.9`'s explicitly-named case answers `TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED` instead — the two cases are opposite shapes, not the same rule applied twice. ⚠️ **Built.** A new `all_topics_names` reads `TopicGrants::topics_for` directly rather than enumerating `Cluster::topic_names` and filtering — doc 15 §4's own cost claim ("O(topics this principal can see), never O(topics that exist)") made real for this path specifically, not just argued: enumerate-then-filter would reintroduce the exact anti-pattern `M9.8`'s index exists to avoid, one call site away from where a reviewer would look for it. Fails open when `credentials_configured` is `false` (`M9.9`'s own signal, no second rule invented); a `None` principal (should be unreachable past `M9.7`'s gate) answers an empty list, not a panic — the same defensive shape `topic_authorized` already used. `resolve_all`'s existing `mode.all_topics` short-circuit needed no change: names from this path are pre-scoped at the source, so skipping the per-entry `topic_authorized` check for them was already correct, not a gap this task had to close. Six tests updated/added in `metadata/tests.rs`: the pre-`M9.10` gap-documenting test (`the_null_topic_array_is_not_yet_scoped`) rewritten to assert the closed behavior (zero grants → zero topics, not every topic in the system) rather than deleted, plus new tests for a partial grant set, the unconfigured fail-open case, the no-principal defensive case, and a correctness check (`M9.17` owns the timing half) that one principal's answer is unaffected by 1,000 unrelated grants existing alongside it. ⚠️ **Round 1 review (changes-requested, 1 major, fixed): `all_topics_names` returned a granted topic's name with no check that it actually existed.** `resolve_all`'s unconditional `resolve_topic` call for `all_topics` entries would then either auto-create it (if `allow_auto_topic_creation`) or answer `UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PARTITION` for a topic the client never named — real Kafka's own null-array path does neither; only an *explicitly-named* topic gets the create-or-refuse treatment, because that is a request the client actually made. Fixed by filtering `all_topics_names`'s own output against `Cluster::partition_count` — one lookup per granted topic (O(this principal's own grant count), never a scan of `Cluster`'s topics, so the cost claim this path exists for stays intact). New test: `a_grant_for_a_topic_that_does_not_exist_is_silently_omitted`, which also asserts the listing itself never creates the topic as a side effect. | M9.12 | Per-principal scoping on produce, fetch, and `ListOffsets` | Serves FR-40. `ListOffsets` specifically needs `M3` (already complete) — doc 02 confirms it is the API `M9.md`'s own "Depends on" section names as untested without it. ⚠️ **Built — `M9.9`'s `AuthzContext`/`topic_authorized` reused, not reinvented.** Both moved from `metadata.rs` to a new shared `authz.rs` (`AuthzContext`, `topic_authorized`), since three more handlers now need them. `Dispatcher` gains one `authz_context(principal)` builder shared by all four scoped handlers (`metadata_handle` refactored onto it too), and each of `metadata_handle`/`listoffsets_handle`/`produce_handle`/`fetch_handle` is its own small method — `dispatch`'s own match arm needed to shrink to fit the fifty-line limit regardless. ⚠️ **Each handler's own shape decided where the check runs**: `produce.rs`'s `one_topic` (before `one_partition`, so a refusal never reaches the ingest rule or the bundle); `listoffsets.rs`'s `answer_all` (a new `refused_partition` helper shared with `one_partition`'s own refusal closure); `fetch/pass.rs`'s `one_topic` (before the budget is spent and before `Spend`/`one_partition` ever touches object storage — reusing `partition::refused` rather than building a fourth refusal shape). `fetch`'s own threading runs through `read_or_park` → `read_all` → `pass::one_topic`, covering both the immediate answer and every re-read pass of a parked fetch with the one change. `None` (unresolvable id, v13+) counts as authorized in both `produce` and `fetch`, so existence-refusal (`UNKNOWN_TOPIC_ID`) keeps its own unmodified meaning at that addressing mode — `M9.10`'s own reasoning applied to three more handlers. `docs/protocol-support.md`'s three rows updated. Tests: unconfigured-fail-open/ungranted-refused/granted-allowed for each of the three handlers (`produce/tests.rs::authorization`, `crates/oqueue-broker/src/fetch/pass.rs::authorization`, `listoffsets/tests.rs::authorization`), plus a refusal-costs-no-GET test for fetch and a refusal-writes-nothing test for produce, plus two end-to-end `Dispatcher`-level tests (`dispatch/tests.rs::authorization`, `Metadata`'s own precedent extended to `Produce`) driving the whole real stack — TLS, credentials, grants, a real `SaslAuthenticate` exchange, then the scoped API — for both `Metadata` and `Produce`. `listoffsets.rs` crossed the 500-line limit with this task's own non-test changes (the `authz` threading, `refused_partition`) and was split, the same mechanical shape used throughout `M9`: `listoffsets.rs` → `listoffsets.rs` + `listoffsets/tests.rs`. ⚠️ **Review (changes-requested, 1 major, fixed): the claim above — "existence-refusal keeps its own unmodified meaning" — held only for `Fetch`'s v13+ (id-addressed) path, and the same asymmetry existed in reverse in `Produce`, unexercised by any new test.** Below v13, `resolved_name`/`topic.name` is the client's raw, unresolved name — never checked against `Cluster::partition_count` — so `topic_authorized` runs directly against it; a topic that was never created and is also ungranted answers `TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED`, not `UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PARTITION`, the opposite of the same logical request at v13+. Traced to a structural cause, not an oversight in either path: `TopicGrants` is keyed by name, so a name-addressed request can be authorized without existence being resolved first (`Metadata`'s own explicit-name case, `M9.9`, does exactly this at every version it serves), while an id has no name to check `can_see` against until it resolves — existence-first is not a policy choice at v13+, it is what makes a name to check exist at all. | M9.14 | Secret and key-material types that cannot reach `Debug`, logs, spans, metric labels, or error variants | Serves FR-44. A static type rule, the first of `M9.15`'s two nets — catches construction, not a hand-rolled interpolation of the bytes (`M9.md`'s own risk bullet: "FR-44 has a gate that cannot be complete," said plainly rather than implied fixed). ⚠️ **Built.** An audit of the whole workspace for secret/key-material-shaped fields found `oqueue_core::Redacted<T>`, `WrappedKey`, `Principal`'s own deliberate non-redaction, and `PlainCredential.password` all already compliant with `security.md` rules 6-7 — with one real violation: `oqueue-codec`'s `SaslAuthenticateRequest`/`SaslAuthenticateResponse.auth_bytes` (`&'a [u8]`, deriving `Debug` directly) carries the RFC 4616 `SASL/PLAIN` triple — password included — in plaintext before `M9.4`'s own parse step splits it, and this codec module cannot itself know which mechanism it is carrying to decide "this one is safe to print." Fixed by wrapping `auth_bytes` in `Redacted<&'a [u8]>` on both types (unconditionally, not only for `PLAIN` — a future mechanism, SCRAM's own proof material say, could put secret bytes on the response side just as easily), `.expose()`d only at the two points that actually need the bytes (`put_bytes` in `encode_response`, `parse_plain` in `oqueue-broker`'s own handler). `Redacted<T>` derives no `Copy`, so both structs' own derive lists dropped it — a small, contained ripple, no call site relied on implicit copy semantics. `scripts/gates/m0-complete.sh`'s hook-count sentences bumped 19→20 as part of the second half of this task below. New `scripts/check-secrets.sh`: `security.md`'s own named static gate, `M9.14` is what wrote it — scans every `struct`/`enum` field declaration in `crates/*/src/` (a brace-depth heuristic, not a real parser, this codebase's own consistent one-field-per-line rustfmt style making that reliable) for a secret-shaped name (`password`/`secret`/`token`/`bearer`/`credential`/`proof`/`auth_bytes`, and their prefixed/suffixed forms) whose type does not contain `Redacted`. Three false positives from the name heuristic recorded in a `NOT_A_SECRET` map, `check-drift.sh`'s own `NOT_A_BOUND` idiom: `authz.rs`'s `credentials_configured: bool` (a flag, not a credential), `dispatch.rs`'s `credentials: Arc<PlainCredentials>` (redacted one level down, inside its own element type), `rate_governor.rs`'s `tokens: u32` (a rate-limiter's bucket count, unrelated to authentication). Negative-tested by hand: reverting `PlainCredential.password` to a bare `String` trips the gate; reverted before commit. Wired into `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. ⚠️ **`AGENTS.md`'s own "some scripts are still missing" paragraph went stale the moment this script landed** — `check-portability.sh`'s own bidirectional check caught it (the exact "M0.1's defect, again" pattern `.agents/skills/README.md`'s analogous section already names for itself) — corrected to state every standards-named script now exists, `check-secrets.sh` named as the last one written, mirroring the skills file's own precedent style. A stale historical illustration inside `check-portability.sh`'s own docstrings (citing `check-secrets.sh` as "written by nobody") corrected to past tense for the same reason, though no gate reads that prose. ⚠️ **Round 1 review (changes-requested, 2 major, 1 minor, fixed).** Major: the name check was `\bWORD\w*\b`, and `\b` cannot see a boundary before `_` — a word character — so `client_secret`/`db_password`/`auth_token` (a compound name more likely in practice than the bare root) were invisible to it. Fixed by replacing it with `name_is_secret_shaped()`: splits the field name on `_` and checks each component against the root list, plus an exact `auth_bytes` substring check. Major: `FIELD_RE` was anchored with `.match()` at line start, so a struct-literal enum variant with more than one field on one line — the reviewer cited this codebase's own `read.rs`'s `Bounded { offset: u64, length: u64 }` as the exact existing shape — only had its first field seen. Fixed by switching to `.finditer()` over the whole line, bounded by the next `,`/`{`/`}`. Minor: `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s own "some gates are still unwritten" qualification was already stale the moment `check-secrets.sh` landed; corrected to say every named gate now exists. Fixing the two majors surfaced two more bugs of my own before this went back for round 2: the first `FIELD_RE` rewrite dropped `\s*` after the `^` anchor, which broke the ordinary indented-field-alone-on-a-line case (caught by negative-testing, since a synthetic violation went silently unflagged); and broadening `token` to a component match newly caught `object_meta.rs`'s `precondition_token` (`ObjectStore`'s own conditional-write opaque token, not a credential), added as a fourth `NOT_A_SECRET` entry after reading `PreconditionToken`'s own doc comment to confirm it is a genuine false positive. Re-verified: `check-secrets.sh` clean on the real tree (141 files scanned), and a git-staged scratch file exercising both a compound-named struct field and a one-line multi-field enum variant was caught by both fixes together, then removed before commit. | done |

| M11.3 | The allocator admits or rejects a producer's sequence before it stages an offset | Serves FR-14; `ADR-0031` points 1, 2, 4 — and `M11.md`'s own task 9 (flush-batcher interaction), which the ADR's `admit`/`stage` split answers directly rather than leaving open. `Allocator` gains `producer_state: HashMap<(ProducerId, TopicId, PartitionId), ProducerState>` beside `end_offsets`. A new `Allocator::admit(spans)` runs *before* `stage` — not inside its existing all-or-nothing loop, because `stage` returns one `Result` for a whole bundled commit and `FR-32` bundles more than one producer's spans into one object, so a check inside `stage` would fail an unrelated producer's offset assignment over one producer's ordinary retry. `admit` partitions spans into: next-in-sequence (forwarded to `stage`, carrying the pending state advance), exact replay (resolved immediately — the *recorded* `base_offset` returned, no offset assigned, no journal touched — the transparent-success case a real duplicate must produce), and rejected (excluded from `stage` entirely, reported on that one `(topic, partition)` independently, exactly the per-partition failure shape a `ProduceResponse` already has). `Allocator::apply` folds an admitted-and-staged producer's state advance on the same all-or-nothing schedule offset writes already use; a fresh `Allocator` (coordinator restart) rebuilds `producer_state` by replaying `MetadataEntry.record`'s producer fields exactly as it rebuilds `end_offsets` — one fold, both lines. Full workspace suite green throughout, `check-mutants` clean. ⚠️ **Review (round 1, one major) found a real gap this note's first version did not**: an all-rejected commit on a coordinator that had never yet published anything left `last_committed`'s `CommitVersion::ZERO` fallback unpublished, and `produce/mod.rs`'s `flush()` observed it onto the session unconditionally — `IndexWatch`'s own `AtLeast` wait requires the index to have applied *something* first, whatever the version, so a session told this fabricated watermark would have its next fetch stall for a write that never happened. Fixed by observing the watermark only when at least one span in the commit was actually assigned an offset — a produce answered entirely in refusals wrote nothing, so it raises no read-your-writes bar at all. New regression test: `an_all_rejected_produce_leaves_the_sessions_watermark_untouched`. | done |

Test: a zombie coordinator (fenced `CoordinatorEpoch`) attempting a producer-sequence commit is refused the same way a zombie's offset commit already is. ⚠️ **Built, on both readings of "epoch bump" the row's own sources carry.** `M11.md` task 10 and `admission.rs`'s own `classify` doc ("a bumped epoch resets the line to zero; a stale one is a zombie") name the *producer's* epoch; `ADR-0031` point 5's prose names `CoordinatorEpoch`. Both are real and neither excludes the other, so both are addressed. **The producer-epoch half (the substantive new mechanism):** `classify` gained two ordered arms before the equal-epoch ones — an incoming epoch *older* than the one on record is `RejectReason::StaleEpoch` (a zombie, real Kafka's `INVALID_PRODUCER_EPOCH`, 47, not an ordinary gap: a retry can never mend it); a *higher* epoch is a legitimate bump, admitted only at its own genuine first sequence (zero), rejected as an ordinary `OutOfOrder` gap otherwise — exactly the `None`-arm rule, restated for a line with history. Only M11.4's non-transactional path mints an epoch at all today, always zero, so a real client cannot yet present a mismatch — this arm exists for the malformed or adversarial one, `security.md` rule 3's "never trust it" applied to a header field like any other. **The `CoordinatorEpoch` half:** genuinely unreachable today and provably so — `coordinator_epoch.rs`'s own doc says failover is `M6`'s and M3-era code elects no replacement, and `Coordinator::open` already refuses a second coordinator over *any* non-empty log unconditionally, before it could answer a sequence check any more than an offset one. No new code needed; a new test (`a_log_carrying_producer_sequence_history_refuses_a_second_coordinator_too`) confirms a log built from a producer-bearing commit is refused open exactly the same way `opening_over_a_log_that_already_holds_entries_refuses` already proves for an offset-only one. `INVALID_PRODUCER_EPOCH` (47) added to `error_codes.rs`, pinned against the dependency, and to `PushOutcome::from_rejection`'s mapping. Doc 06 §6 flags documented librdkafka compatibility gaps for the *retroactive* mechanism specifically — `ADR-0031` does not use that mechanism, but this is still where any gap this design does have would surface, not the unit tests. ⚠️ **Built — two of the three legs by real-client conformance; the third named as provably unreachable that way rather than faked. A genuine defect surfaced and was fixed along the way, corrected below rather than left implicit.** New: `scripts/harness/idempotent_conformance.py`, a third leg in `kafka-client-harness.sh`. It starts its **own** broker with `bin/oqueue serve`'s `advertise` argument pointed at a small frame-aware asyncio TCP proxy it also starts — a transparent Kafka proxy is not actually transparent, since a real client's *actual* work (post-bootstrap) goes wherever `Metadata` advertises, so the proxy has to be what the broker advertises from the very first response, not something spliced in after. The proxy forwards every frame verbatim except the first Produce request: once those bytes are flushed to the broker's own socket, it holds the connection open until the broker's *own response* to that exact request arrives (matched by correlation id), then swallows that response and severs the connection instead of relaying it — `M10.9`'s "ack lost after a durable write" crash, reached here from outside the process. ⚠️ **Gating on the actual response rather than a fixed delay was itself a fix, not the original design**: an earlier version forwarded every broker→client frame unconditionally and raced a `sleep()` against the connection close, on the theory that a local broker's response would always lose that race; independent review actually ran it and found the real ack arrives in well under a millisecond, reaching the client through the unguarded forwarding loop before the sleep-then-close ever fired — the test passed without ever exercising deduplication. ⚠️ **A second, independent defect surfaced while re-verifying the fix**: with the race closed, the delivered offset still came back non-zero on every run. A wire capture (raw bytes, both attempts identical byte-for-byte apart from the correlation id) showed the `RecordBatch` header's `producer_id`/`producer_epoch`/`base_sequence` were all `-1` — the non-idempotent sentinel — and zero `InitProducerId` calls across either attempt. **`M11.md`'s own opening framing and `M11.9`'s commit both assert librdkafka enables idempotence by default; that premise is false** for confluent-kafka's librdkafka (2.15.0, this harness's pinned client) — its actual default is off, and only an explicit `enable.idempotence: True` calls `InitProducerId` at all. Left at the ambient default, the "retry" this test produced was an ordinary at-least-once resend, not idempotent retry logic, and the broker was correctly treating it as a fresh, distinct append — no broker defect, a test-configuration one. Fixed by setting `enable.idempotence: True` explicitly; re-verified against real librdkafka wire traffic that `InitProducerId` now fires and the retry carries the original sequence. `rdkafka_roundtrip.py` carries the same mistaken premise from `M11.9` and is corrected as its own task (`M11.11`), not folded into this diff. The delivered offset is asserted to be the *original* one (0, not 1), and a second, independent lens — a consumer reading straight from the real broker afterward — confirms exactly one record exists, so a duplicate cannot hide behind an offset number alone. **The third leg — "a fenced epoch is refused" — is provably unreachable via any real, standards-compliant non-transactional client**: `M11.4`'s `InitProducerId` handler always mints a fresh id at epoch zero for a non-transactional call, and the only way a real client presents an *existing* id at a *different* epoch is the transactional `InitProducerId` flow, which that same handler refuses outright (FR-15, deferred) — no compliant client can ever be the zombie this leg would need. Named rather than silently dropped: `kafka-client-harness.sh`'s own comment points to `produce/idempotent.rs`'s `a_zombie_epoch_is_refused_with_the_invalid_producer_epoch_wire_code` (`M11.7`) as where that property is verified, at the fidelity actually available — a hand-rolled wire-level client, the same tool `M11.7`'s own admission tests already use for the identical reason. Verified directly, multiple runs: `scripts/docker-test.sh scripts/kafka-client-harness.sh` and `scripts/docker-test.sh scripts/gates/m2-complete.sh` (which calls the harness too) both pass with all three legs green, and the fix was confirmed against a raw wire capture, not just the test's own assertions. | done |

## M10: Deterministic simulation and fault injection

A failing run replays exactly from the seed printed when it failed; the
invariants are checked continuously across a simulated schedule rather than
at its end; and the harness is shown catching something real rather than
merely running. Plan: [milestones/M10.md](milestones/M10.md).
Serves NFR-20 (the method), FR-51 (the method), NFR-21.

⚠️ **It supplies a *method* for NFR-20 and FR-51 rather than meeting them** —
M5, M6 and M15 are where those are verified — and `M10.md`'s Goal says so
plainly rather than borrowing requirement IDs to look conventional.

⚠️ **NFR-21 is different, and `M10.0` moved it here.** `requirements.md` gives
it the verification method "invariant test: the cache is never ahead of
durability", which is `M10.10` and nothing else. M3 owned it and closed with
the substance asserted — `produce/answer.rs`'s "no offset was committed, so
none may be handed out", and `M3.33`'s staged-entry case — but under FR-10's
and FR-11's gate legs, with nothing connecting the requirement to evidence;
M3's addendum review recorded exactly that. ⚠️ **A requirement whose only
verification lives in the *next* milestone cannot be owned by a milestone
being marked complete**, or `check-requirements-trace.sh` reports coverage that
a green gate does not assert. So `M10.15` carries an NFR-21 leg, and the
roadmap's coverage table moves the requirement with the row that verifies it.

⚠️ **M10 is over `sdd.md`'s cap of 20 rows; the argument the standard requires.**
The count is deliberately not written here — `grep -c '^| M10\.'
docs/internal/product/backlog.md` derives it. ⚠️ **Its own decomposition is
under the cap.** What takes it over is what M3 opened after *its* decomposition
and handed on — six rows, one of them three commits' worth and so received as
three (`roadmap.md`'s table, `M10.md`'s intake). That is `M2`'s situation with
M1's eleven and gets the same answer: debt a milestone discovers goes to
whoever opens next, and a receiving milestone that refused it on a count would
be choosing a tidy list over a row that exists. ⚠️ **The test `sdd.md` names is
coherence, not arithmetic**: the received rows are not new scope M10 grew, they
are scope M3 finished discovering, and none of them is simulation work.
⚠️ **And rows a milestone's own reviews open are the other legal addition**,
which `sdd.md` says outright for the *boundary* review: `review.md` rule 16
requires a major finding there to name a backlog row, so a milestone at the cap
has no legal way to act on its own boundary review. ⚠️ **`M10.27` and `M10.28`
are not those** — both come from **per-commit** reviews, whose licence is rule
15a's "a minor worth scheduling sooner is still written as a backlog row in the
next commit", and rule 14 requires neither. The count argument is the same
either way; the citation is not, and a reader who took rule 16 to cover
per-commit findings would conclude every major must open a row, which rules 14
and 15 both say it must not.

⚠️ **The plan's fourteen provisional tasks are re-derived here, not copied**,
and two of them do not survive contact — which `sdd.md` says is the plan
working rather than failing:

- **Lease expiry as an injected fault** (task 7) has no subject. No lease
  exists: `CoordinatorEpoch`'s doc names a leadership lease and nothing
  implements one, and failover is `M6`, which depends on this milestone. The
  *shape* — a node that has lost something and does not know — is built here
  as `M10.8`'s pause; the lease-specific fault goes to `M6` with the lease.
- **A partition between agent and coordinator** (task 8) has no network to
  cut. M3's broker index *is* the coordinator's, folded before the ack by the
  only writer, which is why `Cluster::cache_state` hardcodes `silent_for_ms`
  to zero and why the silence breaker is unreachable. A follower whose index
  is a cache is `M7`'s, and so is this fault.

Both are recorded in `roadmap.md`'s deferral table with receiving milestones,
because `sdd.md` says striking a claim requires naming where the obligation
went and a plan file is not a receiver.

⚠️ **`M10.md`'s one "decision required first" is half-settled and `M10.1` is
the other half.** `M1.22` answered the mechanism — no `madsim` shim exists for
the `reqwest`/`hyper` stack `object_store` reaches the network through, so
there is no `cfg` seam to swap a runtime behind, and `object_store`'s public
`HttpService`/`HttpConnector` seam above the socket is what works. That is
recorded in `testing.md` with its reasoning. What is *not* settled is where
the harness lives in the crate graph, which is the question `#32` actually
asked, and it is expensive to reverse once fourteen rows are written against
it.

`tokio` version it was recorded under, so the corpus stores those beside it or the entries silently stop reaching the interleavings they were recorded for. ⚠️ **Expect sharding to be needed before v1** — doc 19 §9.2 prices the same growth for mutation testing. ⚠️ **The corpus is empty of failures and that is the honest state**, not a broken file: nothing has failed under a seed yet, so the machinery is checked by `--self-test` rather than by pretending an entry exists. ⚠️ **Each row carries the toolchain and `tokio` version it was recorded under**, and a drifted pin is a **warning rather than a failure** — the entry still runs and no longer reaches the schedule it was recorded for, and failing on a toolchain bump would make `build.md` rule 1 impossible while saying nothing would let the corpus become a list of arbitrary numbers. ⚠️ **Replayed in `gates.yml` and not in pre-commit**, because a `cargo test` per entry against `check-budget.sh`'s ten-second ceiling would make a growing corpus fail the budget rather than the thing it watches. ⚠️ **The sweep is nightly and files the seed as an artifact in the corpus's own column order**, so adding an entry is a copy rather than a transcription — a red night that says only "something failed" buys nothing. ⚠️ **And the reader parses with `awk`**: a tab is whitespace to bash's field splitting, so `read -r` with **What a seed varies today is the schedule, not the workload**: the invariant run's steps are written down, so the sweep searches interleavings and `M10.12` is where a generated sequence would come from. ⚠️ **And it took two attempts to make a seed reach anything.** The first read `OQUEUE_SEED` and handed it to `Invariants::for_seed`, which only *labels* a failure; the second routed the run through `run_seeded` and review then measured that the run drew **zero** values from the seeded RNG — `max_wait_ms = 0` makes `park.rs` return before its `select!`, `session.rs` returns before its own, and `connection.rs`'s is off the `Dispatcher` path. The run now parks a fetch against a commit, which reaches `park.rs`'s `select!`, and `the_run_consumes_the_seeded_rng` pins that the draw happens. ⚠️ **What that buys is a *position*, not a divergence**: the two arms are never ready together in this workload — the commit wakes the watch before the paused clock has reason to advance — so branch order changes and the outcome does not. Measured across eight seeds, identical. A workload where the choice is observable is `M10.12`'s. ⚠️ **A set-but-unparseable seed panics** rather than falling back to the default, which is the same failure wearing a green tick. | done |

## M3: Coordinator — offset sequencing and the index

A record is acknowledged only after it is durable in object storage **and**
its position is committed; offsets are monotonic and gap-free per partition
under concurrent producers; a reader resolves offset→object through an index
rather than by listing anything.

⚠️ **"Its position is committed" means committed to an *in-memory* log, and
this file is the artifact that binds** — `sdd.md` makes the backlog the
decomposition and `milestones/M3.md` a hypothesis, so a correction that landed
only in the plan would leave the claim standing in the document `next-task`,
the `milestone` loop and every gate actually read. `FakeMetadataLog` is the
only `MetadataLog` M3 builds; the durable engine is doc 10 #12, which
`ADR-0020` point 5 defers and `roadmap.md` assigns to **M6** (`M6.md` task
7a). So a restarted broker finds an empty log and re-bases at `Offset::ZERO`
over objects that already hold those offsets. ⚠️ **FR-10 is met regardless** —
it says "durable in object storage" and nothing about the metadata log — which
is why `M3.19` recorded this as a scoping correction rather than a milestone
in trouble. Plan: [milestones/M3.md](milestones/M3.md).
Serves FR-10, FR-11, FR-12, FR-13, FR-32, NFR-2, NFR-3. ⚠️ **NFR-21 until
`M10.0`**, which moved it to the milestone holding its only verification —
`M10.10`'s invariant harness; see `M3.md`'s own note and `M10`'s section above.

⚠️ **M3 is over `sdd.md`'s cap of 20 rows; the argument the standard requires.**
The count is deliberately not written here — `grep -c '^| M3\.'
docs/internal/product/backlog.md` derives it, and `sdd.md` says no count a
command can derive goes into prose. Rows fall in four groups. Eighteen are the
decomposition `M3.0` derived from `M3.md`. One (`M3.18`) was a **sweep** row,
the type `ADR-0016` created for review findings worth scheduling before the
milestone-boundary harvest. Two (`M3.19`, `M3.25`) are the checkpoint re-plans
themselves. And the rest come from M3's two mid-milestone reviews: `M3.20`-`M3.24`
are `M3.14` split apart, because that row had accreted five independent
commit-sized changes and become the sole production consumer of everything
`M3.8`-`M3.10` built, which non-negotiable 1 does not permit — one task is one
commit. ⚠️ **Splitting serves the cap rather than evading it**: the limit exists
so a milestone stays reviewable, and one row carrying five commits is less
reviewable than five rows, not more. `M2` set the precedent at larger scale and
made the same argument.

⚠️ **`M3.26`-`M3.38` are the same argument made a second time, against the
sweep row itself.** `M3.25`'s review measured `M3.18` at over twelve hundred
words carrying items from eight commits' reviews, and `sdd.md` is explicit that
a sweep is fixes *sharing a theme* and "is not licence to batch unrelated
scope". What those items shared was a provenance, not a theme: one commit
cannot hold a new fake in `oqueue-core`, a decoder correctness fix over stored
bytes, a codec refusal at nine protocol versions, a gate mechanism, and a dozen
stale sentences. ⚠️ **The split kept every item** — nothing was dropped to make
the count smaller — and moved the obligations that are not M3's work at all to
`roadmap.md`'s deferral table with receiving milestones named. ⚠️ **No number
here.** This said "five", which was wrong, and `sdd.md` forbids writing the
count down at all — so the fix is not a corrected number but a derivation:
count the rows of `roadmap.md`'s deferral table whose second cell names `M3`
as the source. ⚠️ **Not `grep -c '(from M3'`**, which this paragraph
prescribed for one draft and which is wrong twice over: it counts every
`M3`-sourced deferral in the table rather than the ones `M3.25` moved, and it
misses the benchmark-harness row, whose cell reads `from M2 and M3`.

⚠️ **And the same review found M3's rows themselves drifting**, which is why
`M3.26`-`M3.38` are short. `ADR-0016` rule 2 makes a row terse and a `done` row
frozen; M2 held it at a mean of about fifty words a row and M3's mean is four
times that, because every closing commit rewrote its own acceptance cell into
narrative. Prose added at close is prose the per-commit reviewer sees only as
an addition to the row it is judging — which is how `M3.22`'s cell came to
state a charging model its own code inverts (`M3.38`).

order to run, and **every open row is in it** — a sequence that omits one is

| M3.20 | `fetch.max.wait.ms` becomes a real park (from `M3.14`) | Serves FR-12, NFR-2; `M3.md` task 17. M2 parses `max_wait_ms` and discards it; the handler `select!`s `IndexWatch::wait_for` against the request's own deadline — no poll interval, and the timer stays the caller's. The end-to-end case `M3.9` could not write for want of a composer lands here: a fetch racing a concurrent produce sees it, and a fetch at the high watermark issues zero GETs. ⚠️ **Three things it needed that the row did not say.** `oqueue-codec`'s `Fetch` decoder read `max_wait_ms` and `min_bytes` past without keeping them, so the handler had no deadline to honour. `IndexWatch::wait_for` takes a *version*, and a fetch at the watermark cannot name the one it waits for — `wait_past` is the "anything newer than this" the long poll actually needs. And the park is capped at 60 s: `max_wait_ms` is an `i32`, so a client may name twenty-four days, and a broker holding a connection that long is one that never answers rather than one that answers empty — ⚠️ **and it must stay under `ConnectionLimits::idle_timeout`**, or a parked fetch, which sends nothing, is disconnected right after being answered. ⚠️ **Plus the one the review called blocking**: one watch serves every partition on a shard, so a naive re-read on every wakeup turns one parked fetch into an object-storage read per shard *commit*, each of which can be a whole-object GET on the history tier — a client's own request rate stops bounding the broker's read volume. The handler compares watermarks (an index lookup, no GETs) and re-reads only when a partition this request asked about moved, ⚠️ **and reads at most `MAX_READS_PER_REQUEST` times whatever happens** — because `min_bytes` is not always reachable (a page is capped at `MAX_BATCHES_PER_PAGE`, so small batches never fill a megabyte) and commits to the request's *own* partition are legitimate wakeups, so the gate alone leaves the read count set by the producer's rate. ⚠️ **And the watermark baseline is sampled *before* the read, not after**: `read_all` awaits GETs, so a commit landing during it would already be in a baseline taken afterwards — no difference to notice, no version left to wake on, and a fetch that answers at its deadline missing a record that was in the index throughout | done |
| M3.21 | `ListOffsets` and the session watermark: H1 and H2 on the wire (from `M3.14`) | Serves FR-11, FR-12; `ADR-0021`, `ADR-0023`. `ListOffsets(LATEST/EARLIEST)` is always `Linearizable`, routed to the coordinator and never derived from cache — a cached answer reports a log-end-offset below truth and surfaces as **negative consumer lag**. The session carries `CommitAck::watermark()` across requests so a consumer fetching after its own produce is `AtLeast(v)`, and `CacheState::admits` is what decides. Test: produce-then-immediately-consume in one session never sees an empty partition. ⚠️ **`ListOffsets` did not exist**, so this row is also a new API: key 2, v1-9, decoder and encoder hand-rolled and differentialed against `kafka-protocol` both ways, in `ADVERTISED` and therefore in FR-2's matrix. ⚠️ **v0 is excluded because it is a different message** — an array of offsets per partition, pre-KIP-79 — and advertising a version means serving it. ⚠️ **A wall-clock timestamp is refused, not approximated**: there is no index by time, and the nearest offset would send a consumer somewhere it did not ask for in silence. ⚠️ **And the session had nowhere to live**: `Dispatcher` was one shared instance, so it is now built per connection — the scope a client understands, and sharing one would let an unrelated client's produce raise everybody's freshness bar. ⚠️ **Two things the review caught that a first version got wrong, both of the same shape — a mechanism that was decoration.** The `Linearizable` decision was a `debug_assert!` on a condition that is a tautology today, so it was compiled out of release entirely and, when it stopped being a tautology, would have panicked inside a request handler on ordinary client input; it is a `match` now, and the non-`Authoritative` arms refuse rather than answer. And `catch_up` was bounded by the fetch's own `max_wait_ms`, so `fetch.max.wait.ms=0` — every client's non-blocking poll — switched read-your-writes off completely; it is bounded by `ADR-0021`'s staleness budget now, and a promise it cannot keep is an error rather than an empty partition — ⚠️ **`OFFSET_NOT_AVAILABLE` (78), not `LEADER_NOT_AVAILABLE`**, because the Java consumer's fetch error dispatch enumerates 78 and retries while code 5 falls through to an `IllegalStateException` out of `poll()`: a refusal written to protect a client would have killed it | done |
| M3.22 | A 404 is never "end of log": H4's second half, and the reader's byte budget (from `M3.14`) | Serves FR-13, NFR-3, NFR-30; `ADR-0021`, `ADR-0022`. Object ids are never reused, so a 404 means **reaped**, not "not yet written": answer `OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE` on the first miss — ⚠️ **corrected in place by `M3.38`**, which is what the criterion now requires; it said "refresh the index through a coordinator round trip, retry, and only then answer", and no refresh or retry was ever built. Instrument it — a nonzero rate means `M5`'s deletion delay is too short. ⚠️ **And the reader is the real byte budget**: `find_batches` bounds what it can price and may return up to `MAX_BATCHES_PER_PAGE` unpriceable history batches, so the handler stops when its own `max_bytes` fills as it learns each object's size. ⚠️ **And the budget is per *request*, not per partition** (`M3.14`'s review): `fetch.rs`'s `READ_BUDGET_BYTES` is spent once per partition and one `Fetch` frame may name many, so today's bound is partitions × budget with nothing capping the product — and a history read inside it can be up to `MAX_BATCHES_PER_PAGE` whole-object GETs, all concatenated in memory before the response is framed, with `max_in_flight` such requests per connection. ⚠️ **The request's own numbers are not even decoded**: `oqueue-codec`'s `Fetch` decoder reads and discards both `max_bytes` fields, so this row is a codec change and a handler change together. ⚠️ **Built, and the reader's stop is the half `find_batches` cannot do**: a history entry has no byte range to price (`ADR-0022`), so a page can name up to `MAX_BATCHES_PER_PAGE` batches of unknown size — the budget has to be spent as each object's size is *learned*, or a small `max_bytes` still costs sixty-four whole-object GETs. ⚠️ **The first batch is exempt**, as Kafka's own broker has it: a partition whose first batch exceeds the allowance must stay readable, or the consumer parks at that offset forever re-fetching nothing. ⚠️ **And there is no refresh and no retry**, per the correction above: `read_or_refresh` is a passthrough whose own rustdoc says why — in a single-node broker the index a fetch reads *is* the coordinator's, so a second read consults provably identical state and pays a GET for it. Doc 12 §4.6's round trip is `M7`'s, recorded in `roadmap.md`'s deferral table and received by `M7.md` task 17b. ⚠️ **And the bound is on *reads*, not only on bytes**, which review found twice: a partition whose read fails returns nothing, so charging the bytes returned left it free and a client repeating a failing partition still turned one frame into as many object-storage reads as it had entries — measured at 200 GETs for a `max_bytes` of one. The budget is charged what a read *fetched*, and a failed read is charged what it **fetched** — ⚠️ **corrected in place by `M3.38`** under `sdd.md`'s freeze exception, because this cell said "its whole allowance" and the code has never done that: charging the allowance would let one transient fault spend a whole request's budget on bytes nobody has. `M3.26` gave a failed read the bytes it did pull, and `M3.39` stopped it taking the response's overshoot exemption. ⚠️ **Bytes fetched, not bytes returned**, for the same reason at a different scale: a history batch sits inside a bundle covering every partition one flush wrote, so the slice is a fraction of the download | done |

| M3.26 | The reader's object cache and failure cap are per request, not per read pass | Serves FR-13, NFR-3. ⚠️ **Amended while implementing** (`sdd.md`: a spec found wrong is amended and said so): the row asked for `Budget` *and* `FetchedObjects` to span the request, and only the second may. Bytes bound the **response**, which is one pass's outcomes — a budget carried across passes answers a client empty because of bytes it will never see. GETs bound **object storage**, which the whole request pays for. So: the cache and the failure cap span the request, the budget is per pass, and the cache is what stops a per-pass budget starving a re-read, since a second pass over the same offsets is all cache hits. Four parked passes cost `MAX_READS_PER_REQUEST` GETs rather than 1+2+3+4, asserted exactly. A read that fetched an object and then failed to parse it is charged what it fetched and counts against the failure cap — both call sites, tail and history. ⚠️ **And the second amendment, from this row's own review**: a short-circuit answering a target the budget could not reach was written, and the cache in the same change is what falsifies it — a later pass takes everything already fetched for no budget and walks strictly further, so an exhausted budget proves nothing. It is removed rather than narrowed, and `satisfiable_min_bytes` records that what answers the mismatch is the cache plus `MAX_READS_PER_REQUEST`, not arithmetic. | done |

## M2: Kafka wire protocol — produce and fetch

An unmodified Kafka client connects, negotiates versions, produces, and
fetches against a stub partition; "real" is decided by librdkafka. Plan:
[milestones/M2.md](milestones/M2.md). Serves FR-1, FR-2, FR-3.

⚠️ **M2 carries 36 rows, over `sdd.md`'s cap of 20; the argument the standard
requires:** sixteen rows (`M2.2`, `M2.12`-`M2.26`) are the milestone's first
pass at the protocol layer; **eight** (`M2.27`-`M2.34`) are its second — the
protocol-ownership rewrite (`ADR-0019`) the milestone review forced when
`M2.26`'s fuzz harness found a blocking allocation DoS the chosen dependency
could not be made not to have (found debt turned into a decision mid-milestone,
`M1`'s precedent at larger scale); nine (`M2.3`-`M2.11`) absorb the eleven rows
M1 closed `deferred`, the third-bucket reasoning M0→M1 established (carried
debt, not new scope); three (`M2.0`, `M2.1`, `M2.35`) are the opening, the
loop's own repair, and the closing bookkeeping `M1.52`/`M1.57` set the shape
for. ⚠️ The rewrite is the milestone's new center of gravity, not a patch:
`M2.md` records why owning the codec beats bounding the dependency.

⚠️ **Rows here are deliberately terse**: a task, what it serves, an
acceptance criterion, a state. History lives in the commit that closes a
row — `git log --grep <ID>` — not in edits to it; `done` rows are frozen.
`M2.1`'s ADR is to make that the rule and carry the measured argument.

## M1: Object store seam and conformance suite

`ObjectStore` and its three implementations — in-memory (in `oqueue-core`), S3, GCS — plus the
backend-agnostic conformance suite that decides whether the fake can be
trusted. No broker code: this crate is deliberately buildable and testable
without one. Plan: [milestones/M1.md](milestones/M1.md).

⚠️ **M1 carries 59 rows, over `sdd.md`'s cap of 20, and here is the argument
the standard requires.** The milestone is named *Object store seam and
conformance suite*: `M1.1`-`M1.21` are that seam — two ADRs it needs before any
code lands, three real implementations (fake, S3, GCS) sharing one error
taxonomy, one precondition mapping, one retry policy, one rate governor, one
key layout and one conformance suite. None of that is a
second milestone wearing this name — it is the actual size of "three backends
behind one seam, proven equivalent by one suite". `M1.22` is the madsim spike
the plan itself carries as non-code, so it costs a row without costing scope.
`M1.33` through `M1.41` are findings made after this
decomposition was written — a doc-04 citation that does not support what it was
cited for, a CI job that turned out never to have existed, a name-based
threshold matcher whose backstop covers three hardcoded constants, a gate
label pinned by accident, a crate documenting a backend it does not have, a universal claim that outlived its own correction, a wiring comment two backends have overtaken, a budget exemption whose frequency needs a policy before it becomes the norm, and a standard that routed to neither the crate holding every secret nor its own path — so they cost rows without costing scope either. `M1.42`-`M1.45` are the same shape one level up: M1's **milestone** review, which reaches what no per-commit review can, and which found a workspace check that had been red for eighteen commits, a completion gate that never asked whether the milestone was reviewed, an accepted deferral owned by nobody, and three documents still posing questions M1 answered. `M1.46`-`M1.48` are the same again, one layer out: a gate that reported a milestone reviewed when it enumerated nothing, an ADR half-corrected about the seam's own contract, and the discovery that two agent sessions shared one git index with nothing detecting it. `M1.49`-`M1.51` are three more found the same way or while doing the work, each measured rather than argued: non-negotiable 2's canonical wording naming the wrong direction, five `clippy.toml` thresholds pinned by nothing on the commit path, and two pinned container images named twice each with nothing comparing them. `M1.52` is the closing bookkeeping, as `M1.0` was the opening, and `M1.53`-`M1.56` are what M1's *closing* review found, with `M1.57` the row that recorded them — two real defects (`M1.53`'s conditional-write ceiling, `M1.54`'s out-of-bounds range contract), a gate claiming a check nothing performs, and an ADR premise nothing wired. `M1.58`, after the close, is that verdict's three *unowned* minors — two fixed in place, the third moved to `roadmap.md`'s deferral table for `M3`. ⚠️ **All four went `deferred`; | M1.15 | S3 backend: core ops + conditional `PUT` | Serves FR-30, FR-31. `get`/`put`/`delete` against an S3-compatible endpoint using the crate `ADR-0008` chose; conditional `PUT` maps `M1.5`'s `Precondition` to `object_store`'s `PutMode` — this is where the S3 side of `M1.5`'s deferred round-trip test lands, since this is the first code with a real S3 conditional-write encoding to round-trip against; the conformance harness (`M1.10`) registers it and passes against MinIO in CI. Credentials come from the environment, never a literal in code or test fixture (`security.md`). **Also carries `M1.4`'s last remaining dissolved variant**: `Error::Permanent` lands in this commit, the first thing able to produce it (`SlowDown`/`Throttled`/`Transient` moved to `M1.8`'s fault-injection storm instead), plus the classification/mapping layer from `object_store::Error` into all four — a unit test constructs each `object_store`-shaped raw error this backend can actually receive and asserts the classified variant, rather than a shape invented ahead of a real producer. ⚠️ **Also settled the TLS crypto-provider question ADR-0008 deferred to this commit**: `ring`, not `aws-lc-rs` (**ADR-0012**), reached through a feature-only `reqwest`/`rustls` dependency pair plus a runtime `install_ring_provider` call — `object_store`'s and `reqwest`'s own Cargo features cannot express "TLS with `ring`" without also pulling in `aws-lc-rs` somewhere in the graph; the ADR records the mechanism, confirmed by `cargo tree -i aws-lc-sys`/`-i aws-lc-rs` finding neither package and by a real HTTPS round trip under the installed provider. ⚠️ **One documented gap, found writing the conformance test against real MinIO**: a ranged `get` whose *end* runs past the object's true size is checked against `GetResult::range` and correctly raised as `Error::ByteRangeOutOfBounds`, but a range whose *start* is at or past the true size is rejected by `object_store` itself as an unclassifiable `Generic` error before this backend ever sees a size to compare against — it surfaces as `Error::Transient` instead. Closing that needs either an extra `HEAD` per ranged `get` or reaching into `object_store`'s own `pub(crate)` error internals (`error-handling.md` rule 8 already rules out the latter); left as `s3.rs`'s own documented limitation rather than spending `M1.19`'s scope early | done |
| M1.16 | S3 multipart, unconditional | Serves FR-31. ⚠️ **Narrowed before implementation, spec-check step of picking this task up — see ADR-0013.** The row as originally written ("`CompleteMultipartUpload` honours the same `Precondition` as a whole-object `put`") assumed `object_store` exposes a conditional multipart completion publicly; it does not (`CompleteMultipartMode::Create` is `pub(crate)`, used only by the crate's own copy-if-not-exists, not reachable from `oqueue-store` — confirmed against the source and against the open upstream issue `apache/arrow-rs-object-store#289`). What lands here instead: `S3Store::put` splits a payload larger than `MultipartLimits::max_part_size` (S3's real numbers: 5 MiB min part except last, 5 GiB max part, 10,000 max parts, 5 TiB max object) into parts and uploads them via `object_store`'s public `MultipartUpload` API, validated against `M1.9`'s `MultipartSession` before any request is sent — real, exercised capability using `M1.9`'s types, per the original row's intent. `precondition: Some(_)` combined with a payload that size returns `Error::Permanent` rather than silently dropping the precondition. The streaming-writer-with-conditional-seal capability doc 04 §5 actually motivates multipart with is deferred to `M3` (`roadmap.md`'s deferred table, `M3.md` task 19) — it needs a new seam capability `ObjectStore::put`'s complete-in-memory-payload shape cannot express regardless of the `object_store` gap, which is too large for this task and premature before `M3`'s flush batching gives it a real caller. ⚠️ **Review found a second deferral this row's own text had not named**: `M1.14`'s `Operation`/`CountingObjectStore` count one call per `put`, undercounting a multipart `put`'s real request cost (`CreateMultipartUpload` + N `UploadPart`s + `CompleteMultipartUpload`, all one counted `Put` from a decorator wrapping the trait) — `M1.14`'s own comment had assumed this commit would just add a variant, which turned out not to be enough; the actual fix needs a design choice (a contract change, or per-backend accounting) that belongs to `M14`'s API-cost model (NFR-31), not this row — `roadmap.md`'s deferred table, `M14.md` task 5 | done |
| M1.17 | GCS backend | Serves FR-31. ⚠️ **Narrowed before implementation, spec-check step of picking this task up — see ADR-0014.** `GcsStore` implements `get`/`put`/`delete`/multipart via `object_store`'s GCS client (`gcp-base` feature, same `ring`-not-`aws-lc-rs` mechanism ADR-0012/`M1.15` already established); conditional writes map `M1.5`'s `Precondition` to `ifGenerationMatch=0`/`=N` through `PutMode`, encoded via `UpdateVersion::version` rather than `::e_tag` — the one genuinely GCS-specific piece, confirmed against `object_store`'s `gcp/client.rs`; `AlreadyExists`/`Precondition` classification, `get`'s range logic, and the size-based multipart decision are shared with `S3Store` (`crate::classify`/`crate::get`/`crate::multipart`) since none of that logic is actually backend-specific.
